Python Study Guide

A practical path from core language concepts to confident, interview-ready Python — written against Python 3.13.

Who this guide is for

You can write a small script and read other people's code without getting lost. What you want now is the why behind the language: how names and objects work, what really happens when you call a function, how classes look things up, what type hints actually do. This guide takes you from those foundations through functions, decorators, the object model, typing, iteration, errors, testing, and concurrency. It then puts all of that to work in AI applications built on a language model's API — and ends with a working project you build yourself.

If you are starting from zero, you can still use this guide. Chapter 1 assumes no prior Python. The pace picks up from Chapter 2 onward.

What you will be able to do

By the end you will be able to read unfamiliar Python and explain what it does. You will write functions and classes with clear intent, debug reference and scope bugs by reasoning about the object model instead of guessing, and use type hints where they pay off. You will write generators and context managers, handle errors without hiding them, test with the standard library, and reason about threads, processes, and async code at the level interviews expect. You will also call Claude from Python with retries, streaming, validated structured output, tools and concurrency, retrieve documents with vector similarity, and test model-calling code without a network.

What you should know first

Comfort with a terminal and a text editor. No Python experience required. A passing familiarity with any programming language helps but is not assumed.

Python version

This guide is written against Python 3.13 (examples verified on CPython 3.13.16). Where behavior changed between versions, the text says so and links to the official documentation. Anything marked as a CPython detail may differ in other implementations like PyPy.

How to run the examples

Every runnable example in this guide was executed on Python 3.13, and the output shown is the real output. To follow along:

python3 --version        # confirm Python 3.13
python3 example.py       # run a saved example
python3 -m unittest      # run tests (Chapter 7 and the capstone)

You can also paste short examples into the interactive REPL — type python3 with no arguments and you get a prompt where you can try one line at a time. Longer examples are easier to run from files.

How to use this guide

The chapters are ordered by dependency — each one builds on the ones before it. Read them in order the first time. Every major topic follows the same arc: the problem it solves, the mental model, a small runnable example, and a realistic example. Then come edge cases and mistakes, when to use the feature (and when not to), and a practice task with a worked solution. Do the practice tasks. They are where the understanding sticks.

The capstone in Chapter 9 ties everything together in one small command-line program. Build it yourself before reading the worked version.

Key terms appear in a glossary at the end, along with a topic map, a spaced review plan, interview questions, and a checklist confirming every promised topic is covered.

A note on language vs convention

This guide is careful about what is the language versus what is convention. A language rule is enforced by the interpreter. A convention is what experienced Python programmers do (PEP 8 style, underscore prefixes for internals). Third-party tools like mypy or pytest are labeled as such. When the text recommends something, it gives the reason — never "best practice" without one.

Chapter 1: Python Foundations

This chapter builds five ideas carefully, with runnable examples for each. First, how code gets run and how names attach to objects. Then the built-in types, what counts as true, and how control flows through a program. By the end you will read Python the way the interpreter reads it. The surprises in later chapters will be far fewer.

This guide uses Python 3.13 throughout. Where a claim depends on the version, it says so.

1. Running Python: the REPL, scripts, modules, and projects

You need code to run before you can learn anything else. Python gives you three doors into the same interpreter: the interactive REPL for trying things, script files for repeatable work, and modules for sharing code between files. They all execute the same language. They differ only in where the code comes from.

1.1 The REPL: a conversation with the interpreter

REPL stands for read-eval-print loop. You type something, the interpreter reads it, evaluates it, prints the result, and waits for the next line. The prompt is >>>. Anything that is an expression — something with a value — gets its value printed back. Assignments just happen silently.

A sample session looks like this (illustrative transcript):

$ python3.13
Python 3.13.16 (main, ...) on linux
Type "help", "copyright", "credits" or "license" for more information.
>>> name = "Awanish"
>>> name
'Awanish'
>>> len(name)
7
>>> 2 ** 10
1024

Notice the quotes around 'Awanish'. The REPL prints the representation of a value, not the value itself. For strings the representation shows the quotes so you can tell "7" apart from 7. That distinction will matter when you debug.

Use the REPL for trying things: test a slice, check what a method returns, poke at an unfamiliar object. It is a scratchpad, not a workplace. Anything you want to keep belongs in a file. Python 3.13 ships a noticeably better REPL — multi-line editing, syntax coloring, and colorized tracebacks — documented in What's New in Python 3.13.

Two flags extend the REPL's reach. python3.13 -i script.py runs the script and then drops you into an interactive session with all its names still alive. That is handy for inspecting what a script built. python3.13 -c "print(2 + 3)" runs a one-liner without a file.

1.2 Scripts: code that runs top to bottom

A script is a text file ending in .py. The interpreter reads it from the first line to the last and executes each statement in order. There is no separate compile step you must run; Python compiles to bytecode quietly behind the scenes.

"""Chapter 1, example 1: a plain script file.

Run it from a terminal with:
    python3.13 ex-01.py
The interpreter executes the file top to bottom.
"""
name = "Awanish"
print("Hello,", name)
print("2 + 3 =", 2 + 3)
Hello, Awanish
2 + 3 = 5

print() writes its arguments separated by spaces, then a newline. That is the whole contract, and it is enough for most debugging you will do in this guide.

Scripts beat the REPL the moment a task repeats. A script is rerunnable, shareable, and reviewable. The REPL is for questions; scripts are for answers.

1.3 Modules: files that share code

A module is a .py file you import instead of run. Importing executes the file once and binds its top-level names under the module's name. This is how programs stay organized: reusable code lives in modules, and a short driver script sits on top.

Two files make the point. First the module:

"""Chapter 1, example 2 (companion): a module is just a .py file."""

def greet(name):
    return "Hello, " + name + "!"


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(greet("module runner"))

Then the driver:

"""Chapter 1, example 2: importing our own module."""
from pathlib import Path

import ex_02_greeting

print(ex_02_greeting.greet("Awanish"))
print("Loaded from:", Path(ex_02_greeting.__file__).name)
print("greet is a:", type(ex_02_greeting.greet).__name__)
Hello, Awanish!
Loaded from: ex_02_greeting.py
greet is a: function

Three things to take from this. First, import ex_02_greeting runs the module file and gives you its names as attributes — ex_02_greeting.greet. Second, the if __name__ == "__main__": guard distinguishes the two uses of a file. When you run a file directly, Python sets its __name__ to "__main__" and the guarded block executes. When another file imports it, __name__ is the module's own name and the block is skipped. That guard is how one file serves as both reusable module and runnable script. Third, Python finds the module because the script's own directory goes on the import search path automatically. Run the driver from the directory that holds both files and the import just works.

There is also a module-running form: python3.13 -m ex_02 runs the module named ex_02 from the current directory. You will meet -m again with tools like venv and unittest.

The standard library is the same mechanism at scale: hundreds of modules ship with every Python. This guide uses only the standard library. Every import you see — copy, math, pathlib — works on a plain Python 3.13 install with nothing to download. That constraint is deliberate, not a limitation. The standard library covers an enormous amount of ground.

1.4 A basic project layout

Real work needs slightly more scaffolding than one file. A minimal honest layout:

myproject/
    .venv/              # isolated environment (created by venv, not by hand)
    src/
        myapp/
            __init__.py
            main.py
    pyproject.toml      # project metadata (name, version, dependencies)

Two commands create the isolation:

$ python3.13 -m venv .venv
$ .venv/bin/python -c "import sys; print(sys.version)"

A virtual environment is a private copy of the interpreter plus its own package directory. It exists so one project's dependencies never fight another's. The convention — not a language rule — is one environment per project, created with venv, and never committed to version control.

Before running anything, confirm which Python answers. python3.13 --version should print 3.13.x. On some systems python still points at Python 2 or at nothing at all; python3 may point at a different 3.x than you expect. When output surprises you, the interpreter version is the first thing to check.

1.5 When running goes wrong

Four startup failures cover most beginner pain:

  • SyntaxError — the code does not parse. Read the caret: it points at (or just past) the offending token. A missing closing parenthesis on the line above is the classic cause.
  • IndentationError — blocks must line up. Python uses indentation to delimit blocks, and mixing tabs with spaces triggers this.
  • ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'x' — the import search path does not contain x. Usual cause: you ran the script from the wrong directory, so the module's folder was never added to the path.
  • NameError: name 'x' is not defined — you used a name before binding it, or you misspelled it. The REPL forgets everything when it exits; names from yesterday's session are gone.

The tracebacks look hostile at first. Read them bottom-up: the last line names the error, and the lines above show the call chain that led there. In 3.13 the offending expression is often underlined and colorized, which helps.

Practice 1

1.1 — Your first script. Create tip.py. Set bill = 850, compute a 15% tip and the total, and print both. Run it with python3.13 tip.py.

1.2 — Your first module. Move the tip math into billmath.py as a function total_with_tip(bill, pct). Import it in tip.py, guard the runnable part with if __name__ == "__main__":, and verify both python3.13 tip.py and python3.13 -c "import billmath" behave correctly.

Solutions are at the end of the chapter.

2. Names, objects, references, identity, equality, and copying

Here is the single most useful mental model in Python. Get it now and half of the language's "gotchas" stop being gotchas.

The confusion it resolves sounds like this: "I assigned a list to a new variable, changed the new variable, and the old one changed too." That behavior is not a bug. It follows directly from how assignment works. Once you see it, you will predict it every time.

2.1 The mental model: names are labels, objects are things

Two terms carry the whole section:

  • An object is data living in memory, with a type and a value. [1, 2, 3] is an object. So is 42, "hello", and None.
  • A name is a label bound to an object. Names live in namespaces; they are not boxes holding values.

Assignment binds a name to an object. It never copies the object. After a = [1, 2, 3], the name a refers to a list object sitting somewhere in memory. After b = a, the name b refers to the same object. Two labels, one thing. This sharing has a name: aliasing. Changing the object through one name is visible through the other, because there is only one object.

The diagram shows it. a and b both name one list. c names a different list that happens to hold equal values.

The example makes it concrete:

"""Chapter 1, example 3: names, identity, and equality."""
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a            # b names the SAME list object as a (aliasing)
c = [1, 2, 3]    # c names an EQUAL but DIFFERENT list object

print(a == c)    # same contents?
print(a is c)    # same object?
print(a is b)    # same object?

b.append(4)      # mutates the one shared object
print("a is now:", a)

b = [9]          # rebinding b does not touch a
print("a after rebinding b:", a)
print("b:", b)
True
False
True
a is now: [1, 2, 3, 4]
a after rebinding b: [1, 2, 3, 4]
b: [9]

Walk it slowly. b = a binds the name b to the object a already names. b.append(4) mutates that one object, so a sees [1, 2, 3, 4]. Then b = [9] rebinds b to a brand-new list. Rebinding moves the label; it never touches the old object. a still names the original.

This is why "variables" is a slightly misleading word for Python names. A variable in C is a box holding a value. A Python name is a sticky note on an object. When you internalize the sticky-note picture, aliasing bugs become easy to spot: ask "how many objects are there, and which names point at each?"

2.2 Identity vs equality

Two more terms, and the operators that test them:

  • Identity: are these two names pointing at the same object? Tested with is, and id() returns the object's identity number.
  • Equality: do these two objects have equal values? Tested with ==, which asks the objects themselves to compare.

From the example: a == c is True (equal contents), a is c is False (different objects), a is b is True (same object).

The rule for is: use it for singletons, and almost nowhere else. None comes first among them. x is None is the correct None check, and for a reason beyond style. None is a singleton: exactly one None object exists. So identity is the right test, and an object with a strange __eq__ cannot fool it. (PEP 8 recommends is None for the same reason.)

Do not use is to compare numbers or strings. a = 5; b = 5; a is b may be True on CPython. CPython caches small integers (-5 to 256), and it may reuse identical constants compiled together. That is an implementation detail of one interpreter, not a language promise. Another interpreter, or the same interpreter on a different day, may give False. Compare values with ==; compare identity with is. Mixing them up is a real source of bugs that only appear in production.

2.3 Copying: shallow vs deep

Assignment never copies. When you genuinely need a second object, copy explicitly — and know which kind of copy you need.

A shallow copy copies the outer container but shares the inner objects. A deep copy copies the container and everything reachable inside it, recursively. The copy module provides both: copy.copy() and copy.deepcopy(). (Docs: https://docs.python.org/3.13/library/copy.html.)

"""Chapter 1, example 4: shallow vs deep copy."""
import copy

matrix = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
shallow = copy.copy(matrix)
deep = copy.deepcopy(matrix)

shallow[0].append(99)   # inner list is shared with matrix
deep[1].append(100)     # the deep copy owns its own inner lists

print("matrix:", matrix)
print("shallow:", shallow)
print("deep:   ", deep)
print("shallow[0] is matrix[0]:", shallow[0] is matrix[0])
print("deep[0] is matrix[0]:   ", deep[0] is matrix[0])
matrix: [[1, 2, 99], [3, 4]]
shallow: [[1, 2, 99], [3, 4]]
deep:    [[1, 2], [3, 4, 100]]
shallow[0] is matrix[0]: True
deep[0] is matrix[0]:    False

The shallow copy's inner lists are aliases of the original's — appending 99 through shallow shows up in matrix. The deep copy owns independent inner lists, so 100 lands only in deep. The two is checks at the end prove the point: shallow shares, deep does not.

You will also meet three shallow-copy idioms in the wild: a[:], list(a), and d.copy() for dicts. They all copy one level. There is no one-expression deep copy — that is what copy.deepcopy() is for.

A realistic shape of this bug: two parts of a script share a settings dict, and one part "tweaks its own copy":

import copy

defaults = {"retries": 3, "hosts": ["a", "b"]}
service_a = copy.copy(defaults)      # looks independent...
service_a["hosts"].append("c")       # ...but the list is shared

print(defaults)   # {'retries': 3, 'hosts': ['a', 'b', 'c']} -- surprise

The fix is copy.deepcopy(defaults). The diagnosis is the sticky-note question: service_a["hosts"] is defaults["hosts"] — one list, two names.

When to copy at all? Copy when the receiver must be free to mutate without side effects. Do not copy defensively "just in case" — copies cost time and memory, and deep copies of large structures are genuinely expensive. Immutable values (numbers, strings, tuples of immutables) never need copying: they cannot change, so sharing them is always safe. That is one of the quiet payoffs of immutability, and a reason later chapters lean on it.

2.4 Edge cases and diagnosis

  • Rebinding vs mutating. b = [9] moves the label. b.append(9) changes the object. If a bug report says "I changed b and a changed too," check which of the two the code actually did.
  • is with strings. String interning makes some is comparisons accidentally true. Never rely on it.
  • Copying immutables is a no-op. copy.copy(5) is 5 — the module is allowed to return the same object, because there is nothing to protect.
  • The mutable-default-argument trap. This chapter's model explains it, though the full story belongs to the functions chapter. A default like def f(items=[]) binds one list object at definition time, and every call shares it. Same sticky note, many calls.

Practice 2

2.1 — Rebind or mutate? Predict the output, then run it to check:

a = [1, 2]
b = a
b = b + [3]
print(a)
print(b)

Then change the third line to b.append(3) and predict again before running. Explain the difference in one sentence.

2.2 — Shallow surprise. Predict the output, then run it:

import copy
config = {"retries": 3, "hosts": ["a", "b"]}
c2 = copy.copy(config)
c2["hosts"].append("c")
c2["retries"] = 5
print(config)

Then fix it so config is untouched, and state the rule for when deepcopy is required.

3. Core values and types

Python is dynamically typed: names have no types, objects do. x = 3 binds x to an int object; x = "hi" rebinds the same name to a str object. The name never promised anything. This flexibility makes the type system matter more, not less. The checks happen at runtime, on the objects. So you need to know what each type guarantees.

type() tells you an object's type. isinstance(x, int) asks whether x is an int (or a subclass). Prefer isinstance for checks: it respects inheritance, while type(x) == int does not.

3.1 Numbers: int, float, complex

Python has three numeric types, and each solves a different problem.

int is for counting and exact arithmetic. It has arbitrary precision — it grows as large as memory allows. 2 ** 100 computes exactly, no overflow, no wraparound. That is a language guarantee, and it surprises people coming from C or Java, where integers silently overflow.

float is for measurement and scientific computing. On the platforms you will use, it is a 64-bit binary floating-point number. Binary cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly, just as decimal cannot represent 1/3. So 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004, not 0.3. This is not a Python bug. Binary floating point works this way everywhere. Two consequences follow:

  • Never compare floats with ==; use math.isclose(a, b) for "close enough."
  • Never use float for money. Count cents in int, or use decimal.Decimal from the standard library. (That is convention born of hard experience, not a language rule.)

complex is for engineering math: 3 + 4j. The imaginary unit is j, not i. .real, .imag, and abs() (magnitude) cover the basics most people need.

The operators:

Operator Meaning Example Result
+ - * add, subtract, multiply 7 * 6 42
/ true division — always float 7 / 2 3.5
// floor division — rounds down -7 // 2 -4
% remainder — sign follows the divisor -7 % 2 1
** power 2 ** 10 1024
divmod(a, b) quotient and remainder together divmod(7, 2) (3, 1)

Two rows deserve a second look. -7 // 2 is -4, not -3. Floor division rounds toward negative infinity; it does not truncate. And -7 % 2 is 1, not -1. The result takes the divisor's sign, which keeps the invariant (a // b) * b + (a % b) == a true. If you expected C-like truncation, that expectation is the bug.

"""Chapter 1, example 5: numbers."""
print(2 ** 100)
print(7 / 2)
print(7 // 2, -7 // 2)
print(7 % 2, -7 % 2)
print(divmod(7, 2))
print(0.1 + 0.2)
print(round(2.5), round(3.5))   # round-half-even, not "round half up"

z = 3 + 4j
print(z.real, z.imag, abs(z))
1267650600228229401496703205376
3.5
3 -4
1 1
(3, 1)
0.30000000000000004
2 4
3.0 4.0 5.0

One more edge on rounding: round(2.5) is 2 and round(3.5) is 4. Python rounds half to even (banker's rounding), which is the IEEE 754 default. It reduces systematic bias in large aggregations. If your domain needs "half up" — invoicing usually does — use decimal.Decimal with an explicit rounding mode.

3.2 Strings: text you cannot change

A str is an immutable sequence of Unicode characters. Immutable means every "modifying" operation returns a new string; the original never changes. That guarantee is what makes strings safe to share, hash, and use as dict keys.

Indexing starts at 0. Negative indices count from the end. Slices take [start:stop] — start included, stop excluded — and never raise: slicing past the ends just clips. Indexing past the ends raises IndexError. That asymmetry is deliberate: slices are forgiving because they describe ranges; indexing is strict because it names one position.

"""Chapter 1, example 6: strings."""
s = "hello"
print(s[1], s[-1], s[1:4], s[::-1])
print(len(s))

name = "world"
print(f"Hello, {name}! Upper: {name.upper()}")

print(s.replace("l", "L"))   # returns a new string
print(s)                     # the original is unchanged
print("ell" in s)
print("PYTHON".lower(), "  padded  ".strip())
e o ell olleh
5
Hello, world! Upper: WORLD
heLLo
hello
True
python padded

A few notes on the output. s[::-1] reverses via a step of -1; slice syntax is [start:stop:step]. The f-string (f"Hello, {name}!") interpolates expressions inside braces. It is the standard way to build messages, and it beats concatenation for anything beyond the trivial. s.replace returned "heLLo" while s stayed "hello": immutability in action. in tests substring membership.

Strings concatenate with + and repeat with *, but only with strings: "ab" * 3 is "ababab", while "3" + 3 raises TypeError. Python refuses to guess your intent — explicit conversion is required, which section 4.5 covers.

3.3 bytes: data that is not text

str is text: characters. bytes is data: a sequence of integers 0–255. The boundary between them matters everywhere — files, sockets, and HTTP all move bytes; your program thinks in text. Crossing the boundary is explicit:

  • text.encode("utf-8") — text → bytes, using an encoding.
  • data.decode("utf-8") — bytes → text.

UTF-8 is the default encoding and the right choice unless something forces otherwise.

"""Chapter 1, example 7: bytes."""
text = "café"
data = text.encode("utf-8")
print(data, len(data))        # é needs 2 bytes in UTF-8
print(data.decode("utf-8"))

raw = b"\x41\x42"             # hex escapes for byte values
print(raw, list(raw))
print(type(data), type(text))
b'caf\xc3\xa9' 5
café
b'AB' [65, 66]
<class 'bytes'> <class 'str'>

"café" is 4 characters but 5 bytes — the é encodes as two bytes (\xc3\xa9). Character count and byte count are different numbers, and confusing them corrupts data at system boundaries. The b"..." literal writes bytes directly; \x41 is hex for 65, which is ASCII A.

bytes is immutable, like str. Its mutable sibling is bytearray, which you will meet when building binary protocols. Mixing str and bytes in one operation raises TypeError — again, Python refuses to guess the encoding.

3.4 bool and None

bool has two values, True and False. It is a subclass of int: True == 1, False == 0, and True + True is 2. That is language behavior, occasionally useful (counting truthy values with sum()), mostly just something to know.

None is the singleton that means "no value." Functions without a return give back None. Use it as the default "missing" marker, and test it with is None.

"""Chapter 1, example 8: booleans and None."""
x = None
print(x is None)
print(True + True)            # bool arithmetic: 1 + 1
print(True == 1, False == 0)

print(bool(""), bool("False"), bool(0), bool([]), bool(None))
print(bool(" "), bool(0.0), bool([0]))
True
2
True True
False True False False False
True False True

The last two lines are the truthiness rules in miniature: empty things are false, non-empty things are true — with the famous trap in plain sight. bool("False") is True, because the string is non-empty. bool() never reads the content of a string, only whether there is anything there. Section 4.2 states the full rules.

3.5 Lists: the workhorse sequence

Lists are ordered, mutable, and heterogeneous. They are the default collection — reach for a list unless another type's guarantees specifically fit better.

"""Chapter 1, example 9: lists."""
nums = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5]
nums.append(9)
nums.sort()
print(nums)
print(nums.pop(), nums)
print(nums.index(4), nums.count(1))

mixed = [1, "two", 3.0]
print(mixed)
print(mixed[1:], mixed + [True], mixed * 2)
[1, 1, 3, 4, 5, 9]
9 [1, 1, 3, 4, 5]
3 2
[1, 'two', 3.0]
['two', 3.0] [1, 'two', 3.0, True] [1, 'two', 3.0, 1, 'two', 3.0]

The essential methods: append, extend, insert, remove, pop, sort, reverse, index, count. Note the trap: mutating methods return None. nums = nums.sort() assigns None to nums — a classic beginner bug. sort() sorts in place; sorted(nums) returns a new list and leaves the original alone.

Slicing a list returns a new list (a shallow copy of that range). + concatenates, * repeats. in tests membership by equality.

3.6 Tuples: immutable sequences

Tuples are ordered like lists and immutable like strings. That combination makes them the right type for fixed-structure records: coordinates, RGB colors, database rows.

"""Chapter 1, example 10: tuples."""
point = (3, 4)          # packing
x, y = point            # unpacking
print(x, y)

one = (1,)              # tuple
not_a_tuple = (1)       # just parentheses around an int
print(type(one).__name__, type(not_a_tuple).__name__)

print((1, 2) + (3,), (1, 2) * 2)
t = ([1, 2], "tag")     # tuple is immutable, but its items need not be
t[0].append(3)
print(t)
3 4
tuple int
(1, 2, 3) (1, 2, 1, 2)
([1, 2, 3], 'tag')

Unpacking — x, y = point — assigns each element to a name, and it requires the shapes to match. It is one of Python's most-used features; for loops and function returns lean on it constantly.

Two subtleties. First, (1) is just 1 with parentheses; the comma makes the tuple: (1,). Second, tuple immutability is shallow. The tuple t cannot be rebound to different items, but the list inside it can still mutate — and did. Immutability protects the container's structure, not its contents. A tuple is only deeply immutable if everything inside it is too. That is exactly why tuples of strings and numbers work as dict keys.

Use tuples for fixed-shape data and lists for variable-length collections. That convention — records vs collections — is worth adopting early, because it tells readers what to expect.

3.7 Dictionaries: mappings with a memory

A dict maps unique keys to values and remembers insertion order (guaranteed since 3.7 — a language promise you can rely on). Keys must be hashable: immutables like strings, numbers, and tuples of immutables qualify; lists and dicts do not.

"""Chapter 1, example 11: dictionaries."""
scores = {"ana": 92, "dev": 78}
scores["ana"] = 95
scores["kai"] = 88          # new key inserts at the end
print(scores)
print(scores.get("zoe", "absent"))
print(list(scores.keys()), list(scores.values()))

for name, score in scores.items():
    print(name, "->", score)

print("dev" in scores, 95 in scores)   # `in` checks KEYS
{'ana': 95, 'dev': 78, 'kai': 88}
absent
['ana', 'dev', 'kai'] [95, 78, 88]
ana -> 95
dev -> 78
kai -> 88
True False

Reading a missing key with scores["zoe"] raises KeyError. get() avoids that: it returns a default instead. Reaching for get() with a sensible default is the standard defensive read. It exists precisely because missing keys are normal in mapping code, not exceptional.

keys(), values(), and items() return views: live windows onto the dict that reflect later changes. They are iterable and support membership tests. And in on a dict checks keys only — 95 in scores is False even though 95 is a value. That trips people up exactly once.

3.8 Sets: unique items, no order

A set is an unordered collection of unique, hashable items. Duplicates vanish on entry. The payoff is membership testing and the classic set operations — intersection, union, difference — which run fast because sets are hash tables underneath.

"""Chapter 1, example 12: sets."""
tags = {"python", "java", "python"}   # duplicate dropped
print(sorted(tags))
print(sorted({"a", "b"} & {"b", "c"}))   # intersection
print(sorted({"a", "b"} | {"b", "c"}))   # union
print(sorted({"a", "b"} - {"b", "c"}))   # difference
print(sorted({"a", "b"} ^ {"b", "c"}))   # symmetric difference
print(sorted({"banana", "apple"}))       # sorted() gives a stable order

seen = set()
for word in ["cat", "dog", "cat"]:
    seen.add(word)
print(len(seen), sorted(seen))
['java', 'python']
['b']
['a', 'b', 'c']
['a']
['a', 'c']
['apple', 'banana']
2 ['cat', 'dog']

The sorted() calls are load-bearing, not decorative. Set iteration order is not guaranteed — it depends on hashes — so printing a raw set gives unstable output. Sort whenever order matters for display or tests.

Sets deduplicate, which makes them the natural tool for "which distinct X" questions. {} with nothing inside is an empty dict, not a set — use set() for the empty set. And the immutable sibling, frozenset, exists for when a set itself must be hashable (say, as a dict key).

A set of lists raises TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'. Hashability requires immutability in practice: an object whose value can change cannot promise a stable hash. That is the same shallow-immutability idea from tuples, wearing different clothes.

Practice 3

3.1 — Clean and count. Given raw = [" ana", "DEV ", " kai "], build a dict mapping each cleaned, title-cased name to its length: {"Ana": 3, "Dev": 3, "Kai": 3}. Which string methods do you need, and which comprehension shape fits?

3.2 — Bytes round trip. Take text = "naïve café". Encode it to UTF-8 bytes, print the character count and the byte count, decode back, and assert the round trip is lossless. Why do the two counts differ?

4. Mutability, truthiness, comparisons, operators, and conversions

This section collects the rules that sit between the types: which objects can change, what counts as true, how values compare, and how to convert safely. Most Python bugs live here, in the gaps between what code says and what the reader assumed.

4.1 Mutability at a glance

Mutable (can change in place) Immutable (cannot)
list, dict, set, bytearray int, float, complex, bool, str, tuple, bytes, frozenset, None

Mutability is why section 2 matters. Mutable objects can be aliased, so a change through one name is visible through every alias. Immutable objects cannot change, so sharing them is always safe — x = 5; y = 5 can never surprise you.

One caution from section 3.6 bears repeating: immutability is shallow. A tuple holding a list cannot swap the list for something else, but the list itself still mutates. When you need a deeply immutable structure, every level must be immutable.

4.2 Truthiness: what counts as true

Every object can be tested for truth. The falsy values are a short, fixed list:

  • None and False
  • zero of any numeric type: 0, 0.0, 0j
  • empty sequences and collections: "", [], (), {}, set(), range(0)

Everything else is truthy. bool() applies these rules, and if/while apply them implicitly. So if items: means "if items is non-empty." It reads better than if len(items) > 0:, and it is the idiomatic form.

The trap, restated because it bites: bool("False") is True. Truthiness tests emptiness, never content. Parsing "False" into False is a conversion problem, not a truthiness problem — and bool() is the wrong tool for it.

Custom classes can define truthiness with __bool__ (or, failing that, __len__): that is how your own types will plug into these rules later.

4.3 Comparisons

Comparison operators: ==, !=, <, <=, >, >=. Two behaviors to internalize:

Chaining works. 1 < 2 < 3 means 1 < 2 and 2 < 3, with the middle evaluated once. 0 <= n < 100 is the idiomatic range test — clearer than the and version and evaluated efficiently.

Cross-type comparison is strict. == across int and float is fine (3 == 3.0 is True — numeric types compare by value). But "3" == 3 is False, and "3" < 3 raises TypeError. Equality across unrelated types answers "no"; ordering across unrelated types refuses to guess. That asymmetry is deliberate: a wrong order is worse than a wrong equality, because sorting and range checks silently corrupt.

4.4 Operators: logic that returns operands

Arithmetic and comparison operators return values. The logical operators return operands:

  • not x returns a real bool.
  • x and y: returns x if x is falsy, otherwise y.
  • x or y: returns x if x is truthy, otherwise y.

Both short-circuit: evaluation stops as soon as the result is decided, so y may never be evaluated. That makes or the idiom for defaults — name = user_input or "anonymous" — and and the idiom for guards.

The sharp edge: or treats every falsy value as missing. timeout = user_timeout or 30 replaces an explicit 0 with 30. When 0, "", or [] are legitimate values, test explicitly (if user_timeout is not None) instead of reaching for or.

in tests membership (sequences, sets, dict keys). is tests identity (section 2.2). Operator precedence: ** binds tightest, then unary, then *//////%, then +/-, then comparisons, then not, and, or last. When a reader must recall precedence to understand your expression, add parentheses. Clarity beats cleverness.

4.5 Conversions: explicit, each with its own rules

Python converts explicitly. The builtins int(), float(), str(), bool(), list(), tuple(), set(), dict() each implement one crossing, and each has rules worth knowing cold:

"""Chapter 1, example 13: conversion pitfalls."""
print(int("3"), int(3.7), int(-3.7))   # truncates toward zero
print(float("3.5"))
print(bool("False"), bool(""))        # non-empty string -> True
print(str(3) + " apples")             # convert first, then concatenate

try:
    int("3.5")
except ValueError as e:
    print("ValueError:", e)           # try/except catches the error

print(int("0x10", 16), int("101", 2), int("77", 8))
print(list("abc"), tuple([1, 2]), set([1, 1, 2]), str([1, 2]))
3 3 -3
3 3.5
True False
3 apples
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '3.5'
16 5 63
['a', 'b', 'c'] (1, 2) {1, 2} [1, 2]

(The try/except here just catches the error so the script continues; exceptions get their own chapter later.)

The pitfalls, tabulated because you will hit every one:

Expression Result Why
int("3") 3 string parsed as decimal
int("3.5") ValueError int() parses literals, not expressions — no float-shaped strings
int(3.7) / int(-3.7) 3 / -3 truncates toward zero (not floor)
bool("False") True non-empty string is truthy; content ignored
"3" + 3 TypeError no implicit str↔︎int conversion
int(" 42 ") 42 surrounding whitespace is stripped
int("0x10", 16) 16 second argument is the base

Two conversions deserve emphasis. int() on a float truncates toward zero — int(-3.7) is -3, while -3.7 // 1 is -4.0. Different operations, different rules; do not conflate them. And int("3.5") raising is a feature: silent float-to-int coercion would hide data loss, so Python makes you write int(float("3.5")) and own the truncation.

Practice 4

4.1 — Fix and predict. This line raises TypeError: label = "Count: " + 5. Fix it. Then predict each of these before running: bool("0"), int(-2.9), 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3, "7" > 3. For each, name the rule that decides it.

4.2 — The or default. What does x = [] or "default" produce, and why? Give one realistic use of the or-for-defaults idiom and one case where it silently does the wrong thing.

5. Expressions, statements, conditions, loops, match, and comprehensions

This section is control flow: how a program decides what to run next. Two pieces of terminology open it, because Python's own error messages use them.

5.1 Expressions vs statements

An expression is code that produces a value: 2 + 3, "hi".upper(), [x for x in items]. A statement is code that does something: assignment, if, for, return, import. Statements form the skeleton; expressions fill in the values.

The distinction bites in two places. First, you cannot use a statement where an expression is expected. x = (if True: 1) is a SyntaxError, which is why the conditional expression (1 if True else 2) exists. Second, assignment is a statement, so if x = 5: is a SyntaxError too. Python forces you to write ==, and that closes off an entire class of C bugs. (The walrus operator :=, assignment as an expression, is the deliberate exception; later chapter.)

5.2 Conditions

if/elif/else runs the first branch whose condition is truthy. Blocks are delimited by indentation — four spaces by convention — and the colon ends the header line.

"""Chapter 1, example 14: conditions."""
def label(n):
    if n % 2 == 0 and n > 0:
        return "positive even"
    elif n > 0:
        return "positive odd"
    elif n == 0:
        return "zero"
    else:
        return "negative"

for n in [4, 7, 0, -3]:
    print(n, "->", label(n))

print(1 < 2 < 3)                       # chained comparison
print("yes" if 10 > 5 else "no")       # conditional expression

user = ""
greeting = "hello, " + user if user else "hello, stranger"
print(greeting)                        # truthiness drives the choice
4 -> positive even
7 -> positive odd
0 -> zero
-3 -> negative
True
yes
hello, stranger

Order your conditions from most specific to most general. The first truthy branch wins, and later branches never run. The conditional expression a if cond else b is for small value choices, not for logic. If either branch needs more than an expression, write the full if block.

5.3 Loops: for, while, break, continue, else

for iterates over items. It does not count unless you ask it to. range(3) produces 0, 1, 2 for counting, but the idiomatic loop iterates the collection directly: for name in names:. Index-obsessed loops are a habit to unlearn. If you need indices too, enumerate() pairs each item with its index.

while repeats as long as its condition stays truthy. Every while needs progress toward termination inside the body, or it spins forever.

break exits the loop entirely. continue skips to the next iteration. And the loop-else — the clause everyone forgets — runs only when the loop finished without break. It is the natural home for "not found" logic.

"""Chapter 1, example 15: loops."""
for i in range(3):
    print("for:", i)

n = 3
while n > 0:
    print("while:", n)
    n -= 1

def find(items, target):
    for item in items:
        if item == target:
            break
    else:
        return "not found"   # break never fired
    return "found"

print(find([1, 2, 3], 2))
print(find([1, 2, 3], 9))

for i in range(5):
    if i == 3:
        continue             # skip 3, keep looping
    print("kept:", i)
for: 0
for: 1
for: 2
while: 3
while: 2
while: 1
found
not found
kept: 0
kept: 1
kept: 2
kept: 4

The find function shows why loop-else exists. Without it, you would need a flag variable: set found = False, set it True on match, check it after the loop. The else clause says the same thing with no bookkeeping — the else runs exactly when no break fired.

Two loop mistakes to diagnose fast. An infinite while means the condition never became falsy — check that the body actually moves toward termination. And mutating a list while iterating it skips elements or loops oddly; iterate over a copy (for x in items[:]:) when the body removes items.

5.4 match: dispatch on shape

match (3.10+) dispatches on the structure of a value, not just its value. Each case is a pattern; cases try top to bottom; the first match wins; there is no fallthrough. Patterns can match literals, types, sequences by shape, and mappings by key — with case _ as the wildcard and if guards for extra conditions.

"""Chapter 1, example 16: match statements."""
def describe(value):
    match value:
        case int() if value < 0:
            return "negative int"
        case int():
            return "non-negative int"
        case str() if value == "":
            return "empty string"
        case str():
            return "string"
        case [x, y]:
            return f"pair ({x}, {y})"
        case _:
            return "something else"

for v in [-5, 42, "", "hi", [1, 2], None]:
    print(repr(v), "->", describe(v))
-5 -> negative int
42 -> non-negative int
'' -> empty string
'hi' -> string
[1, 2] -> pair (1, 2)
None -> something else

Note the ordering: the guarded case int() if value < 0 must come before the general case int(), because the first match wins. case [x, y] matches any two-element sequence and binds its parts to x and y — that destructuring is the heart of match.

Reach for match when the decision depends on what shape the data has: parsing messages, handling AST nodes, dispatching on message types. Reach for if/elif when the decision depends on arbitrary conditions — ranges, combinations of flags, computed predicates. Shape goes to match; logic goes to if. (Full pattern reference: https://docs.python.org/3.13/reference/compound_stmts.html#the-match-statement.)

5.5 Comprehensions: loops that build collections

A comprehension builds a collection from a loop in one expression: [expr for item in items if condition]. The same shape makes sets ({...}) and dicts ({key: value ...}). A generator expression uses the same syntax with parentheses, but it builds nothing. It yields items lazily, one at a time. That is how you process large streams without materializing them.

"""Chapter 1, example 17: comprehensions."""
squares = [n * n for n in range(6)]
print(squares)

evens = {n for n in range(10) if n % 2 == 0}
print(sorted(evens))

lengths = {word: len(word) for word in ["cat", "window"]}
print(lengths)

total = sum(n * n for n in range(100))   # no list ever built
print(total)

gen = (n * n for n in range(3))
print(type(gen).__name__)                # a generator object, not values
print(list(gen))                        # consuming it yields the values
[0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25]
[0, 2, 4, 6, 8]
{'cat': 3, 'window': 6}
328350
generator
[0, 1, 4]

sum(n * n for n in range(100)) never builds the hundred-element list — the generator feeds squares to sum one at a time. For large inputs that is the difference between fitting in memory and not.

Comprehensions are for building collections from iterations. When the loop body has side effects (printing, appending to multiple structures, complex branching), write the plain loop. A comprehension with side effects reads badly and surprises readers. And when a comprehension needs two nested fors plus a condition, that is usually the signal to write the loop out. One level of nesting with a filter is the sweet spot.

5.6 Putting it together

A word-frequency analyzer uses nearly everything in this chapter. Dicts do the counting, with .get() and a default dodging KeyError. max() takes a key function. A set comprehension filters, sorted() stabilizes the output, and a dict comprehension cross-checks the result.

"""Chapter 1, example 18: putting it together."""
text = "the cat sat on the mat and the cat slept"

counts = {}
for word in text.split():
    counts[word] = counts.get(word, 0) + 1

print(counts)
print("most common:", max(counts, key=counts.get))
print("unique words:", len(counts))

long_words = {w for w in counts if len(w) > 3}
print("long words:", sorted(long_words))

# the same counts as a dict comprehension over the unique words
again = {w: text.split().count(w) for w in set(text.split())}
print("same result:", again == counts)
{'the': 3, 'cat': 2, 'sat': 1, 'on': 1, 'mat': 1, 'and': 1, 'slept': 1}
most common: the
unique words: 7
long words: ['slept']
same result: True

max(counts, key=counts.get) deserves a pause: max over a dict iterates its keys, and key=counts.get scores each key by its count. Two small ideas composing into one line — that compositional habit is the real skill this chapter builds.

Practice 5

5.1 — FizzBuzz. Print the numbers 1–15, but replace multiples of 3 with "fizz", multiples of 5 with "buzz", and multiples of both with "fizzbuzz". Check the multiple-of-both first and say why the order matters.

5.3 — Invert a mapping. Given {"a": 1, "b": 2}, build {1: "a", 2: "b"} with a dict comprehension. When would this lose data?

Practice solutions

1.1

bill = 850
tip = bill * 0.15
print("Tip:", tip)
print("Total:", bill + tip)
Tip: 127.5
Total: 977.5

1.2 — billmath.py:

def total_with_tip(bill, pct):
    return bill * (1 + pct / 100)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(total_with_tip(850, 15))

tip.py:

import billmath

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(billmath.total_with_tip(850, 15))

python3.13 tip.py prints 977.5. python3.13 -c "import billmath" prints nothing — the guard keeps the demo call from running on import, which is exactly what the guard is for.

2.1 — First version: a is [1, 2], b is [1, 2, 3]. b + [3] builds a new list and rebinds b to it; a still names the original. With b.append(3): both are [1, 2, 3], because append mutates the one shared object. The one-sentence version: + rebinds the name to a new object, append mutates the object the name already points to.

2.2 — config prints {'retries': 3, 'hosts': ['a', 'b', 'c']}. The shallow copy shares the inner list, so c2["hosts"].append("c") mutates the original's list. c2["retries"] = 5 only rebinds a key in the copy's own dict. Fix: c2 = copy.deepcopy(config). Rule: reach for deepcopy when the structure contains mutable objects that you will mutate through the copy. Once nesting is involved, one level of copying is not enough.

3.1

raw = ["  ana", "DEV  ", " kai "]
cleaned = [name.strip().title() for name in raw]
result = {name: len(name) for name in cleaned}
print(result)
{'Ana': 3, 'Dev': 3, 'Kai': 3}

strip() removes the surrounding whitespace, title() capitalizes. A list comprehension cleans, a dict comprehension maps each name to its length.

3.2

text = "naïve café"
data = text.encode("utf-8")
print("chars:", len(text), "bytes:", len(data))
assert data.decode("utf-8") == text
print("round trip ok")
chars: 10 bytes: 12
round trip ok

The counts differ because ï and é each take two bytes in UTF-8. Ten characters, twelve bytes — character count and byte count are different numbers, and the encode/decode pair crosses between them losslessly.

4.1 — Fix: label = "Count: " + str(5). Predictions: bool("0") is True — the string is non-empty, and truthiness never reads content. int(-2.9) is -2 — truncation toward zero, not floor. 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is False — binary floating point approximates both sides differently. "7" > 3 raises TypeError — Python refuses to order a string against an int.

4.2 — [] or "default" is "default". or returns its first truthy operand; [] is falsy, so evaluation falls through to "default". Realistic use: name = nickname or "anonymous" — a missing-or-empty input gets a fallback. The silent failure: timeout = user_timeout or 30 discards an explicit 0 (which might mean "no timeout") because 0 is falsy too. When falsy values are legitimate, test with is None instead.

5.1

for n in range(1, 16):
    if n % 15 == 0:
        print("fizzbuzz")
    elif n % 3 == 0:
        print("fizz")
    elif n % 5 == 0:
        print("buzz")
    else:
        print(n)
1
2
fizz
4
buzz
fizz
7
8
fizz
buzz
11
fizz
13
14
fizzbuzz

The multiple-of-both check comes first because 15 is also a multiple of 3. The first truthy branch wins, so an earlier % 3 check would swallow the fizzbuzz case.

5.2

def describe_status(code):
    match code:
        case 200:
            return "ok"
        case 404:
            return "not found"
        case int() if 400 <= code < 500:
            return "client error"
        case int() if 500 <= code < 600:
            return "server error"
        case _:
            return "unknown"

for c in [200, 404, 403, 503, 301, "x"]:
    print(c, "->", describe_status(c))
200 -> ok
404 -> not found
403 -> client error
503 -> server error
301 -> unknown
x -> unknown

404 needs its own case before the 4xx guard, or the guard would claim it. The int() patterns keep non-integer input falling through to unknown instead of crashing the guard's comparison.

5.3

print({v: k for k, v in {"a": 1, "b": 2}.items()})
{1: 'a', 2: 'b'}

It loses data when the original values are not unique: two keys mapping to the same value collapse into one entry, and the later key wins. Inversion is only lossless for one-to-one mappings.

Chapter 2: Functions and Call Behavior

Chapter 1 gave you names, objects, and references. This chapter turns that machinery into the tool you will reach for most: the function. A function packages a computation under a name so you write it once and use it everywhere. The ideas here show up in every Python program you will ever read:

  • how arguments bind to parameters,
  • how names resolve across scopes,
  • how functions remember their surroundings.

Decorators, callbacks, and frameworks you have not met yet all rest on them.

This chapter uses Python 3.13. Most of it has behaved the same for years. Where a feature arrived with a specific version, the text says so.

Defining and calling functions

Every program eventually repeats itself. You validate the same input in three places. You format the same message in five. Each copy is a future bug: you fix one and forget the other. A function solves this by giving the computation a name and a single home. Call the name, and the body runs.

def creates a function object and binds your chosen name to it. Calling the name with parentheses runs the body. The names inside the parentheses in the def line are parameters — placeholders. The values you pass at the call site are arguments — the actual objects.

A function communicates back through return. The return statement ends the call immediately and hands a value to the caller. A return placed before the end of the body is an early return: the rest of the body never runs. If the body finishes without hitting return, the call evaluates to None. That is the implicit None return. It is not an error. It is the defined behavior.

Run this file: code/ch02/ex-01.py.

def greet(name):
    return "Hello, " + name + "!"


def first_positive(numbers):
    for n in numbers:
        if n > 0:
            return n          # early return: stop at the first hit
    return None               # explicit; falling off the end returns None anyway


def log(message):
    print("LOG:", message)    # no return statement: returns None implicitly


print(greet("Awanish"))
print(first_positive([0, -3, 7, -1]))
print(first_positive([0, -3]))
print(log("done"))
print(log("done") is None)
Hello, Awanish!
7
None
LOG: done
None
LOG: done
True

Notice log("done") printed the message and also produced None. print shows that None because we asked it to print the call's result. Beginners often read this as something going wrong. Nothing went wrong. A function that does work and returns nothing still returns None.

Now the Chapter 1 connection. Calling a function passes each argument by object reference — sometimes called call by sharing. The parameter name becomes a second reference to the same object the caller passed. Two names, one object. That means a function can mutate the caller's mutable object, but it can never rebind the caller's name.

Run this file: code/ch02/ex-15.py.

def add_item(cart, item):
    cart.append(item)   # mutates the shared list object -- caller sees this


def reset(cart):
    cart = []           # rebinds only the local name -- caller sees nothing


basket = ["milk"]
add_item(basket, "bread")
print(basket)           # the mutation is visible to the caller
reset(basket)
print(basket)           # the rebinding is not
['milk', 'bread']
['milk', 'bread']

add_item mutates the list both names point to, so the caller sees the change. reset only re-points its own local name at a new list. The caller's name still points at the old one. This distinction — mutating a shared object versus rebinding a name — will explain half the surprises in this chapter.

Common mistakes here are small but worth naming. The classic is forgetting return and then wondering why a variable is None. Another is writing return inside a loop when you meant to collect results. The early return fires on the first iteration, and the loop never finishes. When a function unexpectedly gives None, check two things. Is there a return on every path that should produce a value? And is a return firing earlier than you meant?

Use early returns to flatten nested logic. Instead of indenting the whole body inside if valid:, return immediately when the input is invalid. The main path then sits at the left margin. That shape reads better, and it is the reason early returns exist. Do not use a function where a plain expression will do. Wrapping one line in def adds a name you must remember for no gain.

Try it: write clamp(value, low, high) that returns low when value is below it, high when above it, and value otherwise — using two early returns.

Parameter kinds: positional-only, positional-or-keyword, keyword-only

Arguments arrive at a function in two forms. Positional arguments match parameters by position: compact, but fragile — swap two and nothing complains. Keyword arguments match by name: readable, but verbose. Python lets you control which forms each parameter accepts. This is a language feature, not a style suggestion.

There are exactly three parameter kinds, and two markers in the def line divide them. / marks the end of the positional-only parameters. * marks the start of the keyword-only parameters. Everything between them is positional-or-keyword — the default kind, which accepts either form. The markers are syntax, not parameters. They take no values.

def describe(name, /, age, *, city):

Here name is positional-only, age is positional-or-keyword, and city is keyword-only. The keyword-only marker arrived in Python 3.0; the positional-only marker arrived in Python 3.8 (PEP 570). Both are documented in the Python 3.13 tutorial section on defining functions (https://docs.python.org/3.13/tutorial/controlflow.html).

Why would you restrict how arguments are passed? Positional-only parameters free you to rename them later without breaking callers, and they keep call sites short for identity-like values. Keyword-only parameters force readability at call sites: a bare True tells the reader nothing, but notify=True tells them everything. When you design a function, ask which parameters deserve names at the call site and which do not.

Run this file: code/ch02/ex-02.py.

def describe(name, /, age, *, city):
    # name is positional-only (left of /), city is keyword-only (right of *),
    # age accepts either form.
    return f"{name} is {age}, lives in {city}"


print(describe("Awanish", 48, city="Bridgewater"))
print(describe("Awanish", age=48, city="Bridgewater"))

for call in (
    lambda: describe(name="Awanish", age=48, city="Bridgewater"),
    lambda: describe("Awanish", 48, "Bridgewater"),
    lambda: describe("Awanish", 48, city="Bridgewater", extra="x"),
):
    try:
        call()
    except TypeError as e:
        print("TypeError:", e)
Awanish is 48, lives in Bridgewater
Awanish is 48, lives in Bridgewater
TypeError: describe() got some positional-only arguments passed as keyword arguments: 'name'
TypeError: describe() takes 2 positional arguments but 3 were given
TypeError: describe() got an unexpected keyword argument 'extra'

The error messages are precise, so read them. The second call failed because city sits right of * — it cannot arrive positionally. The third failed because there is no parameter named extra at all.

A realistic case: boolean flags. register(7, "Awanish", True) leaves the reader guessing what True means. Make the flag keyword-only and the call becomes register(7, "Awanish", notify=True). Now every call site shows the flag's purpose. Nobody can silently pass it positionally in the wrong slot. Positional-only fits the other end: an id or a path whose name callers should never depend on. If you later rename user_id to account_id, positional callers keep working.

Edge cases to know: / and * must appear in that order if both are present. A bare * with no name after it is legal — def f(a, *, b) — and simply marks b keyword-only without collecting anything. You cannot give a default to / or * themselves. And keyword-only parameters without defaults are still required; the caller must name them.

Use / when a parameter's name is an implementation detail you want freedom to change. Use * for flags, options, and anything whose meaning is unclear from position alone. Leave ordinary parameters positional-or-keyword — that is the flexible default, and most parameters should stay that way.

Try it: write connect(host, port, /, timeout, *, retries=3, backoff=1.0) and call it three ways — all-positional for the first two parameters, mixed, and one call that fails because a keyword-only argument was passed positionally. Catch the TypeError and print it.

Default values and the mutable-default trap

Some arguments are usually the same. A timeout is usually 30 seconds; a retry count is usually 3. Default values let callers omit the boring arguments and name only what changes. The syntax is name=value in the def line. Parameters with defaults must come after parameters without them. Otherwise a positional call could not know which parameter a value belongs to.

Here is the mental model that prevents the famous bug. The default value expression runs once, when the def statement executes — not on each call. Python stores that object on the function itself and reuses it for every call that omits the argument. For immutable defaults like numbers and strings this is invisible and harmless. For a mutable default like a list, every call shares one list. Each call's appends accumulate in it.

This is not a quirk of some library. It is how def works in the language.

Run this file: code/ch02/ex-03.py.

def add_tag_buggy(tag, tags=[]):
    # The default list is created ONCE, when def runs. Every call that
    # omits tags appends to that same list.
    tags.append(tag)
    return tags


print(add_tag_buggy("a"))   # ['a']       -- looks fine
print(add_tag_buggy("b"))   # ['a', 'b']  -- surprise: 'a' is still there


def add_tag(tag, tags=None):
    # The None sentinel: create a fresh list inside every call.
    if tags is None:
        tags = []
    tags.append(tag)
    return tags


print(add_tag("a"))         # ['a'] -- each call independent now
print(add_tag("b"))         # ['b']
print(add_tag("b", ["x"]))  # ['x', 'b'] -- caller's own list still works
['a']
['a', 'b']
['a']
['b']
['x', 'b']

The standard fix is the None sentinel: default to None, then build the real object inside the body. Each call gets its own list. Callers can still pass their own list, and that keeps working exactly as before. Sometimes None itself is a meaningful value for the parameter. That is rare, but it happens. Then use a private sentinel object instead: _unset = object(), and default to that. Same idea, no ambiguity.

The trap has a quieter cousin. Any expression used as a default is evaluated once at def time, not per call. def f(when=datetime.now()) freezes the time the module was imported, not the time of the call. If the default should be "now", compute it in the body with the sentinel pattern.

Diagnosing this bug: the symptom is state leaking between calls. The function behaves differently the second time with the same inputs. When you see that, look at the def line first. The fix is mechanical: replace the mutable default with None and construct inside. After fixing, re-run the same two calls back to back. The leak disappears.

Use defaults for genuinely optional settings with a sensible usual value. Do not use a mutable object as a default to "accumulate" across calls on purpose. If you need shared state, make it explicit — a module-level name or a class, where the reader can see it. And do not write def f(x=[]) and hope nobody notices. Someone always notices, usually in production.

Try it: write def log_event(event, log=[]) with the bug, demonstrate the leak with two calls, then fix it with the sentinel and show both calls clean.

*args and **kwargs: a variable number of arguments

Sometimes you cannot name every parameter in advance. A report builder takes any number of sections. A decorator must forward whatever arguments the wrapped function takes. *args and **kwargs are the language's answer. In a parameter list, *args collects all extra positional arguments into a tuple. **kwargs collects all extra keyword arguments into a dict. The names args and kwargs are convention; the stars are what matter.

Run this file: code/ch02/ex-04.py.

def make_report(title, *sections, **metadata):
    # *sections collects extra positional args into a tuple;
    # **metadata collects extra keyword args into a dict.
    lines = [title]
    for s in sections:
        lines.append("- " + s)
    for key, value in metadata.items():
        lines.append(f"{key}: {value}")
    return "\n".join(lines)


print(make_report("Shift report"))
print()
print(make_report(
    "Shift report",
    "line 3 down for maintenance",
    "inventory counted",
    author="Awanish",
    shift="night",
))
Shift report

Shift report
- line 3 down for maintenance
- inventory counted
author: Awanish
shift: night

The same function handles zero, two, or twenty sections. The realistic payoff is forwarding: a wrapper that accepts *args, **kwargs and passes them on works with any signature it wraps. You will see this shape constantly in decorators and in library code that wraps user callbacks.

A few precise points. args is a tuple, so it has no append — convert or iterate it. kwargs is a fresh dict per call, so mutating it is safe. The full parameter order in a def line is: positional-only, /, positional-or-keyword, *args, keyword-only, **kwargs. Keyword-only parameters can sit between *args and **kwargs and still require names.

The common mistake is overusing them. When the parameter set is known, name it. def connect(host, port, timeout) tells the reader everything. def connect(*args, **kwargs) tells them nothing, breaks tab-completion, and hides errors until deep inside the body. Reserve *args/**kwargs for genuinely open-ended signatures and for forwarding wrappers. A middle ground exists. Accept the known parameters explicitly, and add **kwargs only for forward-compatible options. Just document what those options are.

Try it: write def shout_all(prefix, *words, sep=" ") that returns prefix + sep.join(words). Call it with zero words and with three.

Unpacking arguments at the call site

The stars work in both directions. In a def line they collect arguments into a tuple or dict. At a call site they unpack one: *iterable spreads an iterable's items as positional arguments, **mapping spreads a mapping's entries as keyword arguments. Same symbol, opposite job. The position tells you which: def line means collect, call site means unpack.

This matters when the data is already packed. Configuration arrives as a dict from a file. Rows arrive as tuples from a database. Unpacking lets you call the function without manually pulling each piece out.

Run this file: code/ch02/ex-05.py.

def launch(host, port, *, timeout=30):
    return f"{host}:{port} timeout={timeout}"


servers = ["db.internal", 5432]   # positional args packed in a list
opts = {"timeout": 5}             # keyword args packed in a dict

print(launch("db.internal", 5432))          # plain call
print(launch(*servers, **opts))             # same call, unpacked at the call site
print(launch("cache.internal", 6379))       # default timeout kicks in

# Binding order: positional fills left to right, then keywords,
# then defaults. A name given twice is an error.
try:
    launch("db.internal", host="db.internal", port=5432)
except TypeError as e:
    print("TypeError:", e)
db.internal:5432 timeout=30
db.internal:5432 timeout=5
cache.internal:6379 timeout=30
TypeError: launch() got multiple values for argument 'host'

The second and first calls are identical. The call site unpacking just moved where the values were assembled. The binding order is strict and worth memorizing:

  1. positional arguments fill parameters left to right,
  2. then keyword arguments fill by name,
  3. then defaults fill whatever is left.

A parameter that gets two values — one positional, one keyword — raises TypeError instead of guessing.

A realistic pattern: dispatch from parsed configuration. You read {"host": ..., "port": ..., "timeout": ...} from a file and call launch(**config). The config keys must match parameter names exactly, which is why clear parameter names matter. One more rule: ** unpacking requires string keys. A dict with non-string keys fails at the call site.

Watch out for mixing unpacking with explicit arguments in confusing orders. f(*a, x=1) is fine and common. f(x=1, *a) is legal too — Python binds positionals first regardless of where they appear in the call. But readability suffers fast. Keep call sites simple: explicit values first, then unpacking.

Use unpacking when the arguments genuinely live in a data structure already. Do not unpack just to avoid typing argument names — launch(host, port, timeout=5) reads better than launch(*pair, **opts) when you know the values at hand.

Try it: given row = ("cache.internal", 6379) and cfg = {"timeout": 2}, write one call to launch that uses both, and predict the output before running.

Scope and name lookup: LEGB

A name can mean different things in different places. The n inside your function is not the n in someone else's. Scope is the region of code where a name binding is visible. Python resolves every name read with the LEGB rule: search the Local scope first, then any Enclosing function scopes, then the Global (module) scope, then the Built-in scope. First hit wins. A miss everywhere raises NameError.

Reading a name searches outward. Writing a name is a different rule, and it trips up almost everyone once. Any assignment to a name inside a function body makes that name local to the whole function body, unless you declare otherwise. Python decides this at compile time, before the function ever runs. So reading the name before the assignment line finds a local name with nothing bound to it yet. The result is UnboundLocalError, not NameError. That error message tells you exactly what happened: the name is local, it just has no value yet.

Two declarations change where assignment writes. global says: this assignment targets the module-level name. nonlocal says: this assignment targets the name in the nearest enclosing function scope that has it. Neither is needed for reading — reads already search outward on their own.

Run this file: code/ch02/ex-06.py.

role = "reader"          # module-level name: the GLOBAL scope
counter = 0


def check():
    level = "local"         # belongs to check: the LOCAL scope

    def inner():
        mode = "innermost"  # belongs to inner: its own local scope
        # lookup: mode in inner, level in the ENCLOSING scope,
        # role in GLOBAL, len in BUILT-IN.
        return mode, level, role, len.__name__

    return inner()


print(check())


def bump():
    global counter          # without this line, counter = counter + 1 would fail
    counter += 1


bump()
bump()
print(counter)


# Assignment creates a local binding even if a global of that name exists.
x = 10


def f():
    # x = 5 below makes x local to f for the WHOLE body,
    # so this read finds nothing assigned yet:
    try:
        print(x)
    except UnboundLocalError as e:
        print("UnboundLocalError:", e)
    x = 5
    return x


print(f())
print(x)                    # the global x is untouched
('innermost', 'local', 'reader', 'len')
2
UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable 'x' where it is not associated with a value
5
10

The realistic use: module-level constants. Define TIMEOUT = 30 at the top of the module and read it freely inside functions — no declaration needed for reading. Functions that need shared writable state are a different story, and that is what the next two sections are really about.

Three sharp edges. First, global on a name that does not exist yet at module level creates it on first assignment. It does not require a prior binding, which surprises people. Second, nonlocal does require the name to exist in an enclosing function scope. Otherwise you get a SyntaxError at definition time. That is actually helpful: it fails fast. Third, UnboundLocalError is a subclass of NameError, so a bare except NameError catches it. When debugging, catch or print the specific subclass so you know which rule you hit.

Use global sparingly. A module-level name that functions mutate is hidden shared state — hard to test, hard to reason about. Prefer passing values as arguments and returning new ones. nonlocal has a cleaner reputation because it belongs to closures, where the enclosing scope is small and visible. You will see it next.

Try it: write a function that reads a module-level TAX_RATE to compute a total, then add a line that assigns TAX_RATE inside the function without global. Predict which error appears and where, then run it.

Nested functions and closures

A function defined inside another function can read the outer function's variables. When the inner function outlives the outer call — returned, stored, passed as a callback — it keeps those variables alive with it. A function bundled with the enclosing bindings it reads is a closure. The variables it captures are free variables: names the inner function uses but does not define.

This solves a real problem: functions that need memory. A counter that remembers its count. A multiplier fixed at creation time. A callback that remembers which button it belongs to. Without closures you would hang that memory on a global or build a class. Closures give you private state with less machinery.

Run this file: code/ch02/ex-07.py.

def multiplier_of(n):
    # multiply remembers n from multiplier_of's scope long after
    # multiplier_of has returned. That remembered access is a closure.
    def multiply(x):
        return x * n
    return multiply


double = multiplier_of(2)
triple = multiplier_of(3)
print(double(5), triple(5))        # 10 15


# THE LATE-BINDING GOTCHA: closures capture VARIABLES, not values.
funcs = []
for i in range(3):
    funcs.append(lambda: i)        # each lambda reads the same live i
print([f() for f in funcs])        # [2, 2, 2] -- i ended at 2

# THE FIX: bind the current value through a default argument.
fixed = []
for i in range(3):
    fixed.append(lambda i=i: i)    # default args are evaluated at def time
print([f() for f in fixed])        # [0, 1, 2]


# Practical closure: a counter that keeps its own private state.
def make_counter():
    n = 0

    def bump():
        nonlocal n                # rebind n in the enclosing scope, not a local
        n += 1
        return n

    return bump


c = make_counter()
print(c(), c(), c())               # 1 2 3
10 15
[2, 2, 2]
[0, 1, 2]
1 2 3

The gotcha deserves a slow reading because it bites everyone. The loop creates three lambdas, but none of them runs during the loop. Each one reads i when called — and by then the loop is over and i is 2. The closures captured the variable, not the value it held at creation time. This is late binding: names in a function body are looked up when the body runs.

The fix exploits the default-value rule from earlier in this chapter: default expressions evaluate once, at def time. lambda i=i: i snapshots the current value of i into a fresh parameter. Each lambda gets its own copy. An alternative fix is a factory function — make_handler(i) in the practice solutions — which gives each closure its own enclosing scope. Both work. Pick the one that reads clearer in context.

The counter shows nonlocal doing its proper job. n lives in make_counter's scope; bump rebinds it there instead of creating a local. Each call to make_counter() builds an independent n, so counters do not share state. No globals involved.

Practical uses go beyond counters:

  • callbacks that remember their context (each button handler remembering its index),
  • decorator factories that remember configuration,
  • small state machines.

Sometimes the state grows past a couple of variables, or needs methods with names. Then a class becomes clearer. Closures are for small, focused memory.

One more caution: closures keep their enclosing scope alive. A closure stored in a long-lived registry pins every variable in that scope. That can hold large objects in memory longer than you meant. If a closure only needs one small value, do not build it inside a scope holding a huge one.

Try it: write make_adder(step) returning a function that adds step to its argument. Create add5 and add10, and show they remember different steps.

Lambda, higher-order functions, and first-class functions

Functions are objects — full citizens. You can store them in lists and dicts, pass them as arguments, and return them from other functions. A function that takes or returns another function is a higher-order function. A lambda is simply a compact way to write a small one. lambda x: x + 1 is a function of one parameter. Its body is the single expression after the colon. It is not a weaker kind of function. It just cannot contain statements.

This matters whenever behavior itself is the parameter. Sorting needs an ordering. Filtering needs a test. A dispatch table needs a handler per key. Passing a function says what to do without hard-coding how.

Run this file: code/ch02/ex-08.py.

# Functions are objects. They can live in data structures...
def greet(name):
    return "Hello, " + name


def shout(name):
    return name.upper() + "!"


handlers = {"greet": greet, "shout": shout}   # stored in a dict
print(handlers["shout"]("awanish"))


# ...and be passed to other functions (higher-order functions).
def apply_twice(fn, value):
    return fn(fn(value))


print(apply_twice(lambda x: x + 1, 10))       # a lambda: a one-expression function


# Realistic: sort key functions. sorted() takes a key FUNCTION.
users = [
    {"name": "awanish", "logins": 41},
    {"name": "neepa", "logins": 128},
    {"name": "shyam", "logins": 7},
]
top = sorted(users, key=lambda u: u["logins"], reverse=True)
print([u["name"] for u in top])
AWANISH!
12
['neepa', 'awanish', 'shyam']

The key argument of sorted is the pattern to internalize. Instead of writing your own sort, you hand sorted a small function that extracts the comparison value. The same shape appears in min, max, filter, and map: a higher-order function doing the traversal, your function supplying the decision.

Edge cases are few but real. A lambda body is one expression — no assignments, no loops, no return keyword (the expression's value is the result). If your lambda grows past one short expression, or you need it in two places, write a def. Naming a lambda — f = lambda x: x + 1 — is discouraged by PEP 8. The reason is concrete. def gives the function a proper name that shows up in tracebacks. A lambda assigned to a variable still reports itself as <lambda> when something fails, which makes debugging harder.

Use lambda for throwaway one-expression functions: sort keys, short predicates, simple callbacks. Use def for anything reused, anything with statements, and anything whose logic deserves a name. Your own higher-order functions may take a function argument. Name that parameter after its role — key, predicate, handler — so callers know what kind of function to pass.

Try it: use filter with a lambda to keep only the users from the example with more than 40 logins, and print their names.

Recursion

Some problems are self-similar: the solution contains a smaller version of the same problem. A directory contains directories. A nested list contains nested lists. Recursion is a function calling itself on the smaller version, plus a base case — an input small enough to answer directly — that stops the descent. Without a base case, the calls never end.

The mental model: each call gets its own fresh set of parameters and local names. factorial(3) calls factorial(2), which calls factorial(1). They are separate invocations sharing only the code, each waiting on the one below it. The base case answers, and the answers combine on the way back up.

Run this file: code/ch02/ex-09.py.

def factorial(n):
    # BASE CASE first: without it, this would call itself forever.
    if n <= 1:
        return n
    return n * factorial(n - 1)   # solve a smaller version of the same problem


print(factorial(5))                # 120


def fib_recursive(n):
    if n < 2:                     # two base cases
        return n
    return fib_recursive(n - 1) + fib_recursive(n - 2)


def fib_iterative(n):
    a, b = 0, 1
    for _ in range(n):
        a, b = b, a + b
    return a


print(fib_recursive(10), fib_iterative(10))
print(len(str(fib_iterative(1000))))   # 209 digits: the recursive one can't reach this depth

import sys
print(sys.getrecursionlimit())    # CPython default: 1000.
                                  # That number is an implementation detail,
                                  # not a promise of the language.
120
55 55
209
1000

The Fibonacci pair makes the trade-off concrete. The recursive version mirrors the mathematical definition and reads beautifully. It is also exponentially slow — fib_recursive(30) makes over a million calls — because it recomputes the same subproblems. The iterative version is linear and handles n = 1000 without blinking. Recursion is not slow in general; this recursion is slow because of repeated work.

Two hard limits. Each call consumes stack space, and Python caps the depth: exceed it and you get RecursionError. The cap is readable via sys.getrecursionlimit(), and it is 1000 by default in CPython. Treat that number as a CPython implementation detail, not a language guarantee. Other implementations may differ, and the language specification does not fix it. Also note that CPython does not optimize tail calls. A recursion a thousand deep is a thousand live frames, no matter how you write it.

When recursion helps: tree-shaped and nested data, such as directory walks, nested JSON, and expression trees. The code follows the data's shape and reads naturally.
