Write the list of dicts to /tmp/ch06_inventory.json with indent=2. Use newline="", encoding="utf-8", and with blocks throughout. The worked solution is at the end of the chapter.

6.8 Logging, debugging, assertions, configuration

print debugging works until the program grows past one terminal. The grown-up toolkit has four parts:

  • logging for observability
  • the debugger for inspection
  • assertions for invariants
  • environment-driven configuration

Logging records what happened, at a severity. The levels, lowest to highest, are DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL. Set the threshold with basicConfig. Get a named logger per module with getLogger(__name__), and log at the level that matches.

basicConfig configures the root logger. Call it once, in your program's entry point, never inside a library module.

# code/ch06/ex-23.py
import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO,           # DEBUG and below are hidden
                    format="%(levelname)s %(name)s: %(message)s")
log = logging.getLogger("orders")                # name it after the module

log.debug("this is hidden: level is INFO")
log.info("order 101 received")
log.warning("stock low for item 7")
log.error("payment failed for order 102")
# logging writes to stderr by default, not stdout
INFO orders: order 101 received
WARNING orders: stock low for item 7
ERROR orders: payment failed for order 102

For production you will want timestamps, file handlers, and structured formats. The logging module supports all of it, and the stdlib docs cover the recipes. The habit to build now: log at the right level, include the values you will need later, and never print in library code.

Debugging starts with the traceback (6.4). Sometimes the traceback is not enough. The traceback module lets you capture one for a handled error and keep going: log it, skip the bad record, continue the loop.

# code/ch06/ex-24.py
"""Log a full traceback for a handled error, then keep going."""
import logging
import traceback

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s: %(message)s")

def divide(a, b):
    return a / b

for a, b in [(10, 2), (10, 0), (8, 4)]:
    try:
        print(f"{a}/{b} =", divide(a, b))
    except ZeroDivisionError:
        logging.error("skipping bad pair:\n%s", traceback.format_exc().strip())
print("done")
ERROR: skipping bad pair:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../ex-24.py", line 12, in <module>
    print(f"{a}/{b} =", divide(a, b))
                        ^^^^^^
  File ".../ex-24.py", line 8, in divide
    return a / b
           ~~^~~
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
10/2 = 5.0
8/4 = 2.0
done

(The ERROR block prints before 10/2 = 5.0 here — stderr versus stdout interleaving again, from 6.5. The program order is correct; only the merged capture shuffles.)

When you need to inspect live state, breakpoint() drops you into pdb, the built-in debugger, at that line. (Set the PYTHONBREAKPOINT=0 environment variable and every breakpoint() becomes a no-op. That's useful when a stray one reaches production.)

The essential commands are p <expr> to print a value, n to run the next line, c to continue, and q to quit. Here is a real pdb session, driven by piped input (paths shortened):

# code/ch06/ex-25.py
def add_up(numbers):
    total = 0
    for n in numbers:
        total += n
        breakpoint()     # drops into pdb here; type `c` to continue, `q` to quit
    return total

print("result:", add_up([1, 2, 3]))
> .../ex-25.py(5)add_up()
-> breakpoint()
(Pdb) 1
(Pdb) > .../ex-25.py(5)add_up()
-> breakpoint()
(Pdb) 3
(Pdb) > .../ex-25.py(5)add_up()
-> breakpoint()
(Pdb) 6
(Pdb) result: 6

Each p total shows the running sum (1, 3, 6), and c resumes until the next breakpoint. pdb has far more commands: l to list source, s to step into calls, w for the stack. But p, n, c, q cover most sessions.

One caution: never commit a breakpoint() to a shared branch. It halts whoever runs the code.

Assertions guard programmer errors, things that must be true if your code is correct. assert condition, message raises AssertionError when the condition fails.

The critical fact: python -O strips all asserts. So asserts are for invariants, never for validating user input or external data. If the check must run in production, raise a real exception.

# code/ch06/ex-26.py
"""assert guards programmer errors. Run with -O and they vanish."""


def discount(price, pct):
    assert price >= 0, f"price must be non-negative, got {price}"
    assert 0 <= pct <= 100, f"pct must be 0-100, got {pct}"
    return price * (1 - pct / 100)


print(discount(100, 20))
try:
    discount(100, 150)   # a bug in OUR code, not bad user input
except AssertionError as e:
    print("AssertionError:", e)

Normal run:

80.0
AssertionError: pct must be 0-100, got 150

With python3.13 -O ex-26.py:

80.0

The second call computed -50.0, and nothing printed it. With -O the asserts vanish. No AssertionError is raised, and the except block never runs. The bug sailed through invisible. That is the whole lesson: asserts are development scaffolding, not validation.

Configuration keeps environment-specific values out of your code. The simplest pattern that scales is to read environment variables with os.environ.get. Always give a default, and convert types yourself, since env vars are strings.

# code/ch06/ex-27.py
"""Configuration from environment variables, with safe defaults."""
import os


def get_config():
    return {
        "host": os.environ.get("APP_HOST", "localhost"),
        "port": int(os.environ.get("APP_PORT", "8000")),   # env vars are strings
        "debug": os.environ.get("APP_DEBUG", "false").lower() == "true",
    }


print("defaults:", get_config())

os.environ["APP_PORT"] = "9000"    # simulate the deploy environment
os.environ["APP_DEBUG"] = "true"
print("from env :", get_config())
defaults: {'host': 'localhost', 'port': 8000, 'debug': False}
from env : {'host': 'localhost', 'port': 9000, 'debug': True}

For a real project, put get_config() in a small config.py module and import it where needed. That gives you one place that knows every setting and its default. Never commit secrets to the repo. They arrive as environment variables from the deploy environment.

(Third-party helpers like python-dotenv load a local .env file into os.environ for development. That is library behavior, not stdlib. It's fine to use; just know which side of the line it sits on.)

Practice task B5. Add observability to a function. Write shipping_cost(weight_kg). It asserts the weight is non-negative and reads a base fee from the SHIP_BASE env var (default "5.0"). It computes base + 1.25 * weight_kg, logs the inputs and result at INFO, and returns the cost. Demonstrate the default and an overridden env value. The worked solution is at the end of the chapter.

6.9 Virtual environments, dependencies, and project layout

Your project needs requests==2.32.3. Another project needs requests==2.28.1. Installing both globally is impossible. This is dependency hell, and virtual environments are the exit.

A venv is a directory with its own Python and its own site-packages. Each project gets one, and their dependencies never meet.

$ ~/.local/bin/python3.13 -m venv /tmp/ch06demo   # create it
$ source /tmp/ch06demo/bin/activate                # use it (Windows: ch06demo\Scripts\activate)
(ch06demo) $ python -c "import sys; print(sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix)"
True

Inside the venv, pip installs into the venv, not the system. A requirements.txt file pins what the project needs, one name==version per line. Then pip install -r requirements.txt reproduces the environment anywhere:

(ch06demo) $ pip install -r requirements.txt
(ch06demo) $ pip freeze > requirements.txt   # snapshot what's installed

Two conventions keep projects sane. The first is layout.

  • A flat layout (myapp.py plus tests/) is fine for small tools.
  • A src layout (src/mypkg/, tests/ at the root) prevents a classic accident: importing the local package instead of the installed one. It is also what packaging tools expect once you publish.

Either way, tests live in a top-level tests/ directory, next to the code, never inside the package.

The second is a reproducible run command. python -m demoapp runs the demoapp package's __main__.py with the project root on sys.path. It's the same invocation on your machine, your teammate's, and CI. It beats python demoapp/__main__.py, which breaks package-relative imports (the 6.6 mistake). Here is a minimal package and the run, executed for real:

# code/ch06/demoapp/__main__.py
"""The package entry point, run as: python -m demoapp"""
import sys


def main():
    print(f"demoapp running on Python {sys.version.split()[0]}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
# code/ch06/ex-28.py
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

print("version:", sys.version.split()[0])
print("in a venv:", sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix)

here = Path(__file__).parent
proc = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-m", "demoapp"],
                      capture_output=True, text=True, cwd=here)
print("--- python -m demoapp ---")
print(proc.stdout, end="")
version: 3.13.16
in a venv: False
--- python -m demoapp ---
demoapp running on Python 3.13.16

And here is the same run inside the fresh venv from above. It proves the environment is truly isolated:

$ /tmp/ch06demo/bin/python -m demoapp
demoapp running on Python 3.13.16
$ /tmp/ch06demo/bin/python -c "import sys; print('in a venv:', sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix)"
in a venv: True

The habit, stated once: one venv per project, dependencies pinned in requirements.txt, tests in tests/, and python -m as the run command. Do that from the first commit, and "works on my machine" stops being a sentence you say.

Practice task B6. From a terminal, work through the venv drill. Create a venv at /tmp/ch06practice and activate it. Confirm sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix prints True. Write a requirements.txt (even an empty one is fine for the drill) and run pip install -r requirements.txt. Then, from code/ch06/, run python -m demoapp with the venv's Python. The worked transcript is at the end of the chapter.

Practice solutions

Solution A1 — EvenNumbers iterator

# code/ch06/sol-01.py
"""Solution A1: an iterator class for even numbers up to a limit."""


class EvenNumbers:
    def __init__(self, limit):
        self.limit = limit
        self.current = 0

    def __iter__(self):
        return self

    def __next__(self):
        if self.current > self.limit:
            raise StopIteration
        value = self.current
        self.current += 2
        return value


print(list(EvenNumbers(10)))
print([n for n in EvenNumbers(7)])
[0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10]
[0, 2, 4, 6]

Try looping over one object twice: ev = EvenNumbers(10); list(ev); list(ev). The second list() is []. Single-pass, as promised.

Solution A2 — running_total generator

# code/ch06/sol-02.py
"""Solution A2: a generator that yields running totals over any iterable."""


def running_total(numbers):
    total = 0
    for n in numbers:
        total += n
        yield total


daily = (sale for sale in [12.5, 7.0, 20.0, 3.5])
print(list(running_total(daily)))
print(list(running_total(range(1, 6))))   # works on any iterable
[12.5, 19.5, 39.5, 43.0]
[1, 3, 6, 10, 15]

Solution A3 — Stopwatch context manager

# code/ch06/sol-03.py
"""Solution A3: a Stopwatch context manager."""
import time


class Stopwatch:
    def __init__(self, label):
        self.label = label

    def __enter__(self):
        self.start = time.perf_counter()
        return self

    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc, tb):
        self.elapsed = time.perf_counter() - self.start
        print(f"{self.label}: {self.elapsed:.4f}s")
        return False   # never swallow exceptions


with Stopwatch("summing") as sw:
    total = sum(range(1_000_000))
print("total:", total)
print("elapsed was positive:", sw.elapsed > 0)
summing: 0.0186s
total: 499999500000
elapsed was positive: True

(The exact elapsed time varies per run; the shape of the output does not.)

Solution B1/B2 — config loader with chaining and boundary catch

# code/ch06/sol-04.py
"""Solution B1/B2: config parsing with a custom exception, chaining,
and catching at the boundary where we can act (log + keep the default)."""
import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.WARNING, format="%(levelname)s: %(message)s")


class ConfigError(Exception):
    """A config line could not be understood."""


def parse_line(line):
    try:
        key, raw = line.split("=", 1)
        return key.strip(), int(raw)
    except ValueError as e:
        raise ConfigError(f"bad config line: {line!r}") from e


DEFAULTS = {"retries": 3}


def load_config(lines):
    config = dict(DEFAULTS)
    for line in lines:
        line = line.strip()
        if not line or line.startswith("#"):
            continue
        try:
            key, value = parse_line(line)
        except ConfigError as e:        # boundary: log it, keep the default
            logging.warning("%s (chained from %r)", e, e.__cause__)
            continue
        config[key] = value
    return config


print(load_config(["retries=5", "timeout=oops", "# comment", "workers=4"]))
WARNING: bad config line: 'timeout=oops' (chained from ValueError("invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'oops'"))
{'retries': 5, 'workers': 4}

Solution B3 — breaking the circular import

The shared module both partners import instead of each other:

# code/ch06/sol05_common.py
"""Solution B3: shared settings live in one module both sides import."""
TIMEOUT = 30
RETRIES = 3
# code/ch06/sol05_a.py
"""Former circular partner A: now depends only on the shared module."""
import sol05_common


def describe_a():
    return f"a uses timeout {sol05_common.TIMEOUT}"
# code/ch06/sol05_b.py
"""Former circular partner B: now depends only on the shared module."""
import sol05_common


def describe_b():
    return f"b uses retries {sol05_common.RETRIES}"
# code/ch06/sol-05.py
"""Solution B3: both partners import the shared module -- no cycle."""
import sol05_a
import sol05_b

print(sol05_a.describe_a())
print(sol05_b.describe_b())
a uses timeout 30
b uses retries 3

Solution B4 — CSV to JSON converter

# code/ch06/sol-06.py
"""Solution B4: CSV -> JSON converter. csv reads strings; convert types."""
import csv
import json
from pathlib import Path

src = Path("/tmp/ch06_inventory.csv")
dst = Path("/tmp/ch06_inventory.json")
src.write_text("sku,qty,price\nA1,10,2.5\nB2,4,9.99\n", encoding="utf-8")

with open(src, "r", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    rows = [{**row, "qty": int(row["qty"]), "price": float(row["price"])}
            for row in csv.DictReader(fh)]

with open(dst, "w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:

Solution B5 — logging, assert, and env config

# code/ch06/sol-07.py
"""Solution B5: logging, assert, and env-var config in one function."""
import logging
import os

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s: %(message)s")
log = logging.getLogger("shipping")


def shipping_cost(weight_kg):
    assert weight_kg >= 0, f"weight must be non-negative, got {weight_kg}"
    base = float(os.environ.get("SHIP_BASE", "5.0"))
    cost = base + 1.25 * weight_kg
    log.info("weight=%.1fkg base=%.2f cost=%.2f", weight_kg, base, cost)
    return cost


print("cost:", shipping_cost(4))
os.environ["SHIP_BASE"] = "7.5"     # simulate the deploy environment
print("cost with env base:", shipping_cost(4))

Chapter 7: Testing, Concurrency, and Practical Reliability

This chapter is about trust. Tests give you a reason to trust your own code. Concurrency lets one program do more at once, but only if you pick the right tool for the kind of work. And a few safety habits keep small programs from becoming security holes. These three topics sit together because they all answer the same question: will this code behave when it matters?

7.1 Unit tests with unittest

Every function you write is a promise: given this input, I produce that output. A unit test is that promise written down so the computer can check it. Without tests, you verify code by running it by hand and eyeballing the result. That works once. It does not work the hundredth time, after six other changes.

Python ships a testing framework in the standard library: unittest. It needs no install and no setup. A test is a method on a class that inherits from unittest.TestCase. Each method whose name starts with test becomes one test. Inside, you call the code and check the result with assertion methods like assertEqual.

Two more terms before the example. A fixture is the known starting state a test needs. Here, that's a fresh bank account with 100 in it. setUp builds the fixture before every test method, and tearDown cleans up after. Each test gets its own fixture, so tests cannot pollute each other.

code/ch07/ex-01.py:

"""unittest basics: descriptive test names, setUp/tearDown fixtures.

Run with:  python3.13 ex-01.py
"""
import unittest


class BankAccount:
    """A tiny account class — the code under test lives in the same file
    here so the example is self-contained."""

    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0.0):
        if balance < 0:
            raise ValueError("opening balance cannot be negative")
        self.owner = owner
        self.balance = balance

    def deposit(self, amount):
        if amount <= 0:
            raise ValueError("deposit amount must be positive")
        self.balance += amount
        return self.balance

    def withdraw(self, amount):
        if amount <= 0:
            raise ValueError("withdrawal amount must be positive")
        if amount > self.balance:
            raise ValueError("insufficient funds")
        self.balance -= amount
        return self.balance


class TestBankAccount(unittest.TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        # Runs before EVERY test method: each test gets a fresh account.
        self.account = BankAccount("Asha", balance=100.0)

    def tearDown(self):
        # Runs after EVERY test method: tidy up the fixture.
        self.account = None

    def test_deposit_increases_balance(self):
        self.account.deposit(50.0)
        self.assertEqual(self.account.balance, 150.0)

    def test_withdraw_decreases_balance(self):
        self.account.withdraw(30.0)
        self.assertEqual(self.account.balance, 70.0)

    def test_withdraw_exact_balance_leaves_zero(self):
        # Edge case: withdrawing everything should be allowed.
        self.account.withdraw(100.0)
        self.assertEqual(self.account.balance, 0.0)

    def test_opening_with_negative_balance_raises(self):
        # assertRaises also works in the old "callable" form:
        # pass the callable and its arguments separately.
        self.assertRaises(ValueError, BankAccount, "Ravi", -10.0)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main(verbosity=2)

Output:

test_deposit_increases_balance (__main__.TestBankAccount.test_deposit_increases_balance) ... ok
test_opening_with_negative_balance_raises (__main__.TestBankAccount.test_opening_with_negative_balance_raises) ... ok
test_withdraw_decreases_balance (__main__.TestBankAccount.test_withdraw_decreases_balance) ... ok
test_withdraw_exact_balance_leaves_zero (__main__.TestBankAccount.test_withdraw_exact_balance_leaves_zero) ... ok

----------------------------------------------------------------------
Ran 4 tests in 0.000s

OK

Notice the test names. They read as sentences: deposit increases balance, opening with negative balance raises. When one fails months from now, the name tells you what broke without opening the file. test1, test2 tell you nothing. Name the behavior, not the method.

A realistic note on placement. In a real project the BankAccount class would live in its own module (say bank.py), and the test file would import it. Keeping both in one file here is a teaching shortcut, so the example runs as-is.

Edge cases and common mistakes

The most common unittest mistake is a test that never runs. If the method name does not start with test, the runner silently skips it. The symptom is unmistakable once you know it. The summary says Ran 0 tests and everything is "OK," because nothing ran. Always glance at the test count.

The second most common mistake is a fixture that leaks. If setUp builds one shared object and a test mutates it, the next test starts from dirty state and fails for no honest reason. setUp runs before every method precisely so each test starts clean. Treat the fixture as disposable.

A subtler one: testing three behaviors in one method. When it fails, you get one failure and three suspects. One behavior per test method. Tests are cheap; debugging is not.

When do you not need unittest? For a ten-line throwaway script, a quick REPL check is fine. The moment code gets reused, imported, or edited more than once, tests pay for themselves. For tiny checks there's a simpler alternative: plain assert statements in a scratch script. They are not a test suite, but they beat eyeballing.

7.2 Testing exceptions and edge cases

Happy-path tests check that correct input gives correct output. The bugs live at the edges: zero, empty, negative, one-too-many. And sometimes the exception is the behavior. A function that should reject bad input is only correct if it actually rejects it.

unittest checks expected exceptions with assertRaises. You saw the callable form in the last example. The more flexible form is a context manager. The code inside the with block must raise, and you get the exception object back to inspect.

code/ch07/ex-02.py:

"""Testing exceptions and edge cases: assertRaises as a context manager,
checking the error message, and boundary values.

Run with:  python3.13 ex-02.py
"""
import unittest


def apply_discount(price, percent):
    """Return price after a percent discount (0-100)."""
    if price < 0:
        raise ValueError("price cannot be negative")
    if not 0 <= percent <= 100:
        raise ValueError("percent must be between 0 and 100")
    return price * (1 - percent / 100)


class TestApplyDiscount(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_typical_discount(self):
        self.assertAlmostEqual(apply_discount(200.0, 25), 150.0)

    def test_zero_percent_is_full_price(self):
        # Edge case: boundary of the allowed range.
        self.assertAlmostEqual(apply_discount(80.0, 0), 80.0)

    def test_hundred_percent_is_free(self):
        # Edge case: the other boundary.
        self.assertAlmostEqual(apply_discount(80.0, 100), 0.0)

    def test_negative_price_raises(self):
        # Context-manager form lets you inspect the raised exception.
        with self.assertRaises(ValueError) as ctx:
            apply_discount(-5.0, 10)
        self.assertIn("negative", str(ctx.exception))

    def test_percent_above_100_raises(self):
        with self.assertRaises(ValueError) as ctx:
            apply_discount(50.0, 101)
        self.assertIn("between 0 and 100", str(ctx.exception))

    def test_percent_below_0_raises(self):
        with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
            apply_discount(50.0, -1)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main(verbosity=2)

Output:

test_hundred_percent_is_free (__main__.TestApplyDiscount.test_hundred_percent_is_free) ... ok
test_negative_price_raises (__main__.TestApplyDiscount.test_negative_price_raises) ... ok
test_percent_above_100_raises (__main__.TestApplyDiscount.test_percent_above_100_raises) ... ok
test_percent_below_0_raises (__main__.TestApplyDiscount.test_percent_below_0_raises) ... ok
test_typical_discount (__main__.TestApplyDiscount.test_typical_discount) ... ok
test_zero_percent_is_full_price (__main__.TestApplyDiscount.test_zero_percent_is_full_price) ... ok

----------------------------------------------------------------------
Ran 6 tests in 0.000s

OK

A few things are worth noticing.

  • The boundary tests (0% and 100%) probe exactly where the allowed range ends. Off-by-one errors love boundaries.
  • assertAlmostEqual compares floats with a tolerance, because 0.1 + 0.2 style arithmetic rarely lands exactly.
  • ctx.exception lets you check the message, not just the type. Otherwise a ValueError raised for the wrong reason would pass your test.

The classic assertRaises mistake is writing self.assertRaises(ValueError, apply_discount(-5.0, 10)). That calls the function immediately. The exception fires before assertRaises ever runs, and your test errors instead of passing. Pass the callable and its arguments separately, or use the with form. The with form is easier to read, and it's the one you will reach for most.

So when should you test exceptions? Test the errors your callers depend on. If your function's contract says "raises ValueError on bad input," that contract deserves a test. Do not test that Python itself raises TypeError when someone passes a string where you do arithmetic. That is Python's behavior, not yours.

7.3 pytest — optional third-party

Everything so far used only the standard library. pytest is different: it is a third-party package, not part of Python. You install it with pip install pytest. This guide's baseline stays unittest because it works everywhere with zero setup. But you will meet pytest in real codebases, so you should recognize it.

What pytest adds over unittest:

  • Plain assert statements. No assertEqual, no assertIn. You write assert result == 150.0, and when it fails pytest shows you the values on both sides. Less to memorize, clearer failures.
  • Fixtures as function arguments. Instead of setUp methods, a @pytest.fixture function builds the input and the test receives it as a parameter.
  • pytest.mark.parametrize. One test function runs once per row of a table — a dozen cases with no copy-paste.
  • A huge plugin ecosystem (coverage, async tests, and more). That is third-party territory; the core above is what matters first.

code/ch07/ex-03.py — run it with python -m pytest ex-03.py -v:

"""The same idea as the unittest examples, written with pytest
(a THIRD-PARTY library — install it first:  pip install pytest).

pytest needs no TestCase class and no assertX methods: plain `assert`
statements do the checking, and fixtures supply test data.

Run with:  python -m pytest ex-03.py -v
"""
import pytest


def apply_discount(price, percent):
    if price < 0:
        raise ValueError("price cannot be negative")
    if not 0 <= percent <= 100:
        raise ValueError("percent must be between 0 and 100")
    return price * (1 - percent / 100)


@pytest.fixture
def price():
    """A fixture is pytest's version of setUp: it builds the input
    each test needs and hands it over as a function argument."""
    return 200.0


def test_typical_discount(price):
    assert apply_discount(price, 25) == pytest.approx(150.0)


def test_hundred_percent_is_free(price):
    assert apply_discount(price, 100) == pytest.approx(0.0)


def test_negative_price_raises():
    # pytest.raises is the context manager for expected exceptions.
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="negative"):
        apply_discount(-5.0, 10)


@pytest.mark.parametrize("percent, expected", [(0, 200.0), (50, 100.0), (100, 0.0)])
def test_discount_table(price, percent, expected):
    """parametrize runs the same test once per row — a whole table
    of cases with no copy-paste."""
    assert apply_discount(price, percent) == pytest.approx(expected)

Output (pytest 9.1.1):

cachedir: .pytest_cache
rootdir: /home/hatch/workspace/build/python-study-guide/code/ch07
collecting ... collected 6 items

ex-03.py::test_typical_discount PASSED                                   [ 16%]
ex-03.py::test_hundred_percent_is_free PASSED                            [ 33%]
ex-03.py::test_negative_price_raises PASSED                              [ 50%]
ex-03.py::test_discount_table[0-200.0] PASSED                            [ 66%]
ex-03.py::test_discount_table[50-100.0] PASSED                           [ 83%]
ex-03.py::test_discount_table[100-0.0] PASSED                            [100%]

============================== 6 passed in 0.08s ===============================

pytest.approx is pytest's answer to assertAlmostEqual: float comparison with tolerance. The match="negative" argument checks the exception message with a regex, like inspecting ctx.exception in unittest.

Reach for pytest in any real project where you control the environment. Its failure output alone is worth the install. Stay with unittest in locked-down environments where you cannot install packages, or in codebases already written in unittest style. The two can coexist in one repo, but pick one per project.

Learning unittest first is the right order. It teaches the concepts (cases, fixtures, assertions) that pytest then makes more convenient.

7.4 Threads, processes, and asyncio — the conceptual map

"Concurrency" means making progress on more than one thing at a time. Python gives you three tools, and picking the wrong one is the classic beginner trap. The choice depends on one question: what is the work waiting on?

Threads share one process and one memory space. The catch is the GIL, the Global Interpreter Lock. It means only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time.

That sounds like threads are useless. But the GIL is released while a thread waits, whether on a network response, on disk, or on a lock. So threads shine for I/O-bound work. Ten threads downloading files genuinely overlap, because each spends most of its life waiting with the GIL released.

One version note, scoped carefully. Python 3.13 added experimental support for running without the GIL. These "free-threaded" builds are usually invoked as python3.13t (see What's New in Python 3.13, PEP 703). The feature is experimental and not the default. The standard python3.13 you installed keeps the GIL, and everything in this chapter assumes that.

Processes (the multiprocessing module) sidestep the GIL completely. Each process is its own Python interpreter with its own memory and its own GIL, so they truly run in parallel on multiple cores.

The price is real. Processes are heavy to start, they cannot share memory directly, and data passed between them gets pickled. Use them for CPU-bound work: image processing, compression, number crunching.

asyncio takes a third path: one thread, one process, but many tasks that cooperate. Each task runs until it hits an await, which means "I'm waiting, run someone else." The event loop then switches to another task. There are no GIL fights, no process overhead, and no shared-memory races. It scales to thousands of concurrent waits.

The price: your code must be written in async style throughout, and one blocking call freezes the whole loop.

The interview-level summary fits in a table:

Workload Waiting on Reach for
Downloading 200 files network I/O threads or asyncio
Resizing 200 images CPU multiprocessing
Chat server, 10k connections many concurrent waits asyncio
Crunching numbers in pure Python CPU multiprocessing (threads won't help — GIL)

The example below makes the GIL concrete. Part 1 simulates eight network calls; part 2 does pure-Python arithmetic. Watch threads win part 1 and tie part 2.

code/ch07/ex-04.py:

"""Threads: great for I/O-bound work, useless for CPU-bound work (GIL).

Part 1: eight simulated network calls. Sequential vs threads.
Part 2: pure-Python number crunching. Sequential vs threads.
Watch what the GIL does to part 2.

Run with:  python3.13 ex-04.py
"""
import threading
import time


def fake_network_call(name, results):
    time.sleep(0.2)  # stand-in for waiting on a socket / API response
    results.append(name)


def crunch(n):
    total = 0
    for i in range(n):  # pure Python: holds the GIL the whole time
        total += i * i
    return total


def run_threaded_io():
    results = []
    threads = [threading.Thread(target=fake_network_call, args=(f"job-{i}", results))
               for i in range(8)]
    for t in threads:
        t.start()
    for t in threads:
        t.join()
    return sorted(results)


def run_threaded_cpu():
    out = [None, None]

    def worker(i):
        out[i] = crunch(2_000_000)

    threads = [threading.Thread(target=worker, args=(i,)) for i in (0, 1)]
    for t in threads:
        t.start()
    for t in threads:
        t.join()
    return out


print("--- I/O-bound: 8 x 0.2s simulated network calls ---")
start = time.perf_counter()
results = []
for i in range(8):
    fake_network_call(f"job-{i}", results)
print(f"sequential: {time.perf_counter() - start:.2f}s")

start = time.perf_counter()
run_threaded_io()
print(f"8 threads:  {time.perf_counter() - start:.2f}s  (threads overlap the waiting)")

print("--- CPU-bound: 2 x crunch(2_000_000), pure Python ---")
start = time.perf_counter()
crunch(2_000_000)
crunch(2_000_000)
print(f"sequential: {time.perf_counter() - start:.2f}s")

start = time.perf_counter()
run_threaded_cpu()
print(f"2 threads:  {time.perf_counter() - start:.2f}s  (GIL: no real parallelism)")

Output:

--- I/O-bound: 8 x 0.2s simulated network calls ---
sequential: 1.60s
8 threads:  0.20s  (threads overlap the waiting)
--- CPU-bound: 2 x crunch(2_000_000), pure Python ---
sequential: 0.33s
2 threads:  0.31s  (GIL: no real parallelism)

Eight network calls drop from 1.6s to 0.2s, because the waits overlap. The number crunching takes the same time with or without threads. The GIL lets only one thread compute at a time, so you paid the threading overhead for nothing. (Your exact timings will differ slightly run to run. What matters is the shape: big win versus no win.)

Each tool has its common mistake.

  • With threads: mutating shared data without a lock. Two threads updating one counter can silently lose updates (a race condition).
  • With processes: spawning a process pool for a millisecond of work. The startup cost dwarfs the job.
  • With asyncio: calling a blocking function like time.sleep() or a synchronous HTTP library inside a coroutine. It freezes every task on the loop. The async equivalent of sleep is await asyncio.sleep().

Sometimes you need none of them. If the program is fast enough sequentially, keep it sequential. Concurrency adds failure modes: races, deadlocks, tasks that never finish. Simple code you can reason about beats clever code you cannot.

7.5 async/await: one complete example

Here is the mental model for asyncio in a few sentences. A coroutine is a function defined with async def that can pause itself. await is the pause button. It says: "suspend me until this slow thing finishes, and let other tasks run meanwhile." The event loop is the scheduler. It watches all paused tasks and wakes each one when its wait is over. asyncio.run() builds the loop, runs your top-level coroutine, and closes everything down.

Three more terms for the example.

  • A Task wraps a coroutine so the loop can schedule it independently (asyncio.create_task).
  • asyncio.gather runs several coroutines concurrently and returns their results in order.
  • asyncio.wait_for sets a deadline. If the task is not done in time, it gets cancelled and TimeoutError is raised.

(Since Python 3.11, asyncio.TimeoutError is the builtin TimeoutError, so there's one name to catch.)

code/ch07/ex-05.py:

"""async/await: one complete example.

- asyncio.sleep stands in for real I/O (a network call, a DB query).
- asyncio.gather runs several coroutines concurrently on ONE thread.
- asyncio.wait_for cancels a task that takes too long -> TimeoutError.
- Exceptions inside tasks are handled where the task is awaited.

Run with:  python3.13 ex-05.py
"""
import asyncio
import time


async def fetch(name, delay):
    """Pretend to fetch something over the network."""
    print(f"  start {name} (will take {delay:.1f}s)")
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)  # yields control back to the event loop
    print(f"  done  {name}")
    return f"{name}: {delay:.1f}s"


async def slow_fetch():
    await asyncio.sleep(5.0)
    return "this line never runs"


async def flaky_fetch():
    await asyncio.sleep(0.2)
    raise ConnectionError("server reset the connection")


async def main():
    print("1) gather: three fetches run concurrently")
    started = time.perf_counter()
    results = await asyncio.gather(
        fetch("users", 0.5),
        fetch("orders", 0.3),
        fetch("stock", 0.4),
    )
    print("   gathered:", results)
    print(f"   took {time.perf_counter() - started:.2f}s, not 0.5+0.3+0.4 = 1.2s\n")

    print("2) wait_for: cancel a task that is too slow")
    try:
        await asyncio.wait_for(slow_fetch(), timeout=1.0)
    except TimeoutError:  # asyncio.TimeoutError is the builtin TimeoutError
        print("   slow_fetch cancelled -> TimeoutError after 1.0s\n")

    print("3) exceptions: handle them where you await the task")
    tasks = [
        asyncio.create_task(fetch("ok-page", 0.2)),
        asyncio.create_task(flaky_fetch()),
    ]
    for task in tasks:
        try:
            print("   task result:", await task)
        except ConnectionError as exc:
            print("   task failed:", exc)


asyncio.run(main())
print("event loop closed, program exits")

Output:

1) gather: three fetches run concurrently
  start users (will take 0.5s)
  start orders (will take 0.3s)
  start stock (will take 0.4s)
  done  orders
  done  stock
  done  users
   gathered: ['users: 0.5s', 'orders: 0.3s', 'stock: 0.4s']
   took 0.50s, not 0.5+0.3+0.4 = 1.2s

2) wait_for: cancel a task that is too slow
   slow_fetch cancelled -> TimeoutError after 1.0s

3) exceptions: handle them where you await the task
  start ok-page (will take 0.2s)
  done  ok-page
   task result: ok-page: 0.2s
   task failed: server reset the connection
event loop closed, program exits

Read the output like the loop does. All three fetches start before any finishes. Each await asyncio.sleep hands control back, so the loop starts the next one. They finish in order of their delays (orders, stock, users). But gather returns results in the order you passed them. Total time is 0.5s, the longest wait, not the sum. That is the whole payoff of async I/O.

Two exception details are worth keeping.

First, wait_for cancels the slow task. It does not keep running in the background. Cancellation is how you enforce deadlines: "answer in one second or I stop waiting."

Second, an exception inside a task surfaces when you await that task. If you never await it, the exception sits unretrieved and Python warns you at shutdown. A practical rule: every task you create gets awaited somewhere, with handling where it makes sense.

One more gather behavior for the road. By default, the first exception raised by any of the gathered coroutines propagates out of gather immediately, and the other results are lost. If you want every result including failures, pass return_exceptions=True. Exceptions then come back as values in the results list instead of being raised. (That is stdlib behavior, not style advice.)

Async is sometimes the wrong tool. CPU-bound work gains nothing on one thread. A script with two sequential steps gains nothing but syntax. Mixing needs care too. If a library only offers blocking calls, run it in a thread from async code with asyncio.to_thread() rather than calling it directly. That keeps the loop responsive.

7.6 Performance: think in big-O, measure, then do less

Performance work has an order of operations, and skipping steps is how people waste afternoons. First, think about the algorithm: how does the work grow as the input grows? Then measure to find where time actually goes. Then, and only then, optimize. The honest rule behind all of it: most speedups come from doing less work, not from doing the same work faster.

Big-O is the vocabulary for "how does the work grow." O(n) means doubling the input roughly doubles the work: one pass over the data. O(n²) means doubling the input quadruples the work: a loop inside a loop. The difference looks academic at n=10 and brutal at n=10,000.

Big-O describes growth, not seconds. An O(n²) algorithm can still win on tiny inputs. It is a thinking tool for choosing approaches, not a stopwatch.

The example finds duplicate order IDs two ways. Same answer, different growth.

code/ch07/ex-06.py:

"""Performance: the algorithm decides first, the profiler shows where,
and doing less work is the real speedup.

Find duplicate order IDs two ways, time them with time.perf_counter,
then profile the slow one with cProfile.

Run with:  python3.13 ex-06.py
"""
import cProfile
import pstats
import random
import time


def dupes_slow(order_ids):
    """O(n^2): for each id, scan the whole list for a match."""
    dupes = []
    for i, oid in enumerate(order_ids):
        for other in order_ids[i + 1:]:
            if oid == other and oid not in dupes:
                dupes.append(oid)
    return dupes


def dupes_fast(order_ids):
    """O(n) average: one pass, a set remembers what we have seen."""
    seen, reported, dupes = set(), set(), []
    for oid in order_ids:
        if oid in seen and oid not in reported:
            reported.add(oid)
            dupes.append(oid)
        seen.add(oid)
    return dupes


random.seed(42)
order_ids = [random.randint(1, 50_000) for _ in range(4_000)]
order_ids += order_ids[:200]  # sprinkle in 200 duplicates

start = time.perf_counter()
slow = dupes_slow(order_ids)
slow_time = time.perf_counter() - start

start = time.perf_counter()
fast = dupes_fast(order_ids)
fast_time = time.perf_counter() - start

assert sorted(slow) == sorted(fast)  # same answer, wildly different cost
print(f"O(n^2) version: {slow_time:.3f}s, found {len(slow)} duplicates")
print(f"O(n)   version: {fast_time:.3f}s, found {len(fast)} duplicates")
print(f"speedup: {slow_time / fast_time:.0f}x from changing the algorithm alone\n")

print("cProfile on the slow version (top functions by total time):")
profiler = cProfile.Profile()
profiler.enable()
dupes_slow(order_ids)
profiler.disable()
pstats.Stats(profiler).sort_stats("tottime").print_stats(4)

Output:

O(n^2) version: 0.548s, found 321 duplicates
O(n)   version: 0.000s, found 321 duplicates
speedup: 1270x from changing the algorithm alone

cProfile on the slow version (top functions by total time):
         323 function calls in 0.287 seconds

   Ordered by: internal time

   ncalls  tottime  percall  cumtime  percall filename:lineno(function)
        1    0.286    0.286    0.287    0.287 /home/hatch/workspace/build/python-study-guide/code/ch07/ex-06.py:15(dupes_slow)
      321    0.000    0.000    0.000    0.000 {method 'append' of 'list' objects}
        1    0.000    0.000    0.000    0.000 {method 'disable' of '_lsprof.Profiler' objects}

That's a 1270x speedup with zero cleverness. The fast version just does less work. A set lookup is O(1) on average, so one pass replaces the nested scan. (Timings jitter run to run; the gap between the two approaches does not.)

Then comes the profiler. time.perf_counter() is the right clock for quick before/after timings. Unlike time.time(), it is monotonic and high-resolution.

cProfile answers the harder question: which function is slow. Read its table by the tottime column. That's the time spent in the function itself, excluding calls it makes. Here dupes_slow owns 0.286 of 0.287 seconds. No mystery, no guessing: the nested loop is the whole story.

The realistic connection: this is the same set-membership idea from the data-structures chapters, now paying rent. Every in check against a list inside a loop is a quiet O(n) hiding inside your O(n). Reach for a set or dict when you test membership repeatedly.

Performance work has its own common mistakes:

  • Optimizing before measuring. The slow part is rarely where you feel it is.
  • Micro-tuning the wrong function, such as saving microseconds in code that runs once.
  • Benchmarking sloppily. One run on a busy machine proves little. Compare approaches on the same machine, and distrust tiny differences.

So when should you optimize? Optimize the hot path the profiler identified, and only when the speed matters to someone: a user waiting, a bill growing, a batch missing its window. Code that runs in 0.000s, like the fast version above, is done. Readability wins every tie.

7.7 Safety habits: eval, pickle, and their safer replacements

Two stdlib features can run attacker code if you hand them untrusted input. Both are safe with data you produced yourself. Both are dangerous with data from users, files you did not write, or anything off the network. Know the mechanism and the replacement.

Never eval() untrusted input. eval takes a string and executes it as Python code. That is its entire job. Any part of that string might come from outside your program: a form field, a config file, an API response. If it does, treat it as hostile. An attacker can put anything in it, and eval will run it with your program's permissions.

Never unpickle untrusted data. pickle.loads rebuilds objects from bytes. Here is the mechanism. A pickled object can carry a __reduce__ method telling pickle which callable to invoke to reconstruct it. Pickle invokes it during loads(). So an attacker crafts bytes whose __reduce__ points at os.system or similar, and merely unpickling runs their command. The file extension does not matter; the bytes are the program.

code/ch07/ex-07.py:

"""Safety: never eval() untrusted input, never unpickle untrusted data.

Both execute attacker code. The demos below are deliberately harmless
(getcwd / print) — a real attacker would run anything they want.

Safer alternatives: ast.literal_eval for Python literals, json for data.

Run with:  python3.13 ex-07.py
"""
import ast
import json
import os
import pickle

print("=== 1. eval() runs whatever string it is given ===")
print("eval('2 + 3 * 4') ->", eval("2 + 3 * 4"))

# An attacker-controlled string reaches the real operating system:
payload = "__import__('os').getcwd()"
print("eval(payload) reached the OS and returned:", eval(payload))
print("Harmless here — but the payload could have been os.system('...').\n")

print("=== 2. pickle.loads() runs code hidden in the bytes ===")


class Sneaky:
    def __reduce__(self):
        # __reduce__ tells pickle how to rebuild the object.
        # Attackers return (some_function, (args,)) — and pickle
        # CALLS it during loads(). Here it just prints.
        return (print, ("*** code executed during pickle.loads() ***",))


blob = pickle.dumps(Sneaky())  # an attacker emails you this blob
print("Unpickling attacker bytes:")
pickle.loads(blob)
print()

print("=== 3. Safe alternatives ===")
print("ast.literal_eval:", ast.literal_eval("[1, 2, {'a': 3}]"))
print("json.loads:      ", json.loads('{"user": "asha", "admin": false}'))

for bad in ["__import__('os').getcwd()", "{1, 2, 3} | {4}"]:
    try:
        ast.literal_eval(bad)
    except (ValueError, SyntaxError) as exc:
        print(f"literal_eval refused {bad!r}: {type(exc).__name__}")

Output:

=== 1. eval() runs whatever string it is given ===
eval('2 + 3 * 4') -> 14
eval(payload) reached the OS and returned: /home/hatch/workspace/build/python-study-guide/code/ch07
Harmless here — but the payload could have been os.system('...').

=== 2. pickle.loads() runs code hidden in the bytes ===
Unpickling attacker bytes:
*** code executed during pickle.loads() ***

=== 3. Safe alternatives ===
ast.literal_eval: [1, 2, {'a': 3}]
json.loads:       {'user': 'asha', 'admin': False}
literal_eval refused "__import__('os').getcwd()": ValueError
literal_eval refused '{1, 2, 3} | {4}': ValueError

The payload string called a real OS function through eval. There was no exploit trickery, just what eval does. The pickle demo printed from inside loads(), before your program ever touched a result. Both prove the same point: these functions do not distinguish data from instructions.

The replacements cover the legitimate uses:

You need Use Why it is safe
Parse a Python literal ("[1, 2]", "{'a': 3}") from a string ast.literal_eval Only builds literals — strings, numbers, lists, dicts. Refuses calls, imports, operators.
Exchange structured data (configs, API payloads) json Parses data, never executes it.
Serialize your own objects for later pickle Fine — but only unpickle bytes you produced yourself.

Two caveats are worth stating plainly.

ast.literal_eval is not a general expression evaluator. "{1,2} | {3}" fails because set union is an operation, not a literal. That refusal is the safety.

And json cannot represent every Python object: no tuples-as-tuples, no datetimes, no custom classes. That limitation is also the safety. When you need richer types across a boundary, define a schema and validate. Do not reach back for eval.

When do these rules not apply? eval on a string your own code constructed from constants, in a REPL or a debugger, is fine. The danger is untrusted input, not the function. Pickle between two programs you wrote, over a channel you control, is the standard use. The rule is about trust boundaries. User input, uploaded files, network data, and third-party feeds are untrusted until validated.

7.8 Practice tasks

Five tasks, one per topic. Work each before reading its solution — the solutions are at the end of this chapter.

Task 1 — testing. The function below turns a title into a URL slug. Write a unittest.TestCase with at least five tests. Cover a basic case, punctuation handling, multiple spaces, leading/trailing junk, and the empty string. Run it and confirm all pass.

import re

def slugify(title):
    """Turn 'Hello, World!' into 'hello-world' for use in URLs."""
    slug = title.lower()
    slug = re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9]+", "-", slug)
    return slug.strip("-")

Task 2 — asyncio. Write an async program that greets three people concurrently. Each greeting takes a different simulated time. Any greeting slower than 0.5 seconds should be skipped with a "timed out" message instead of failing the whole program. Use asyncio.gather, asyncio.wait_for, and per-task exception handling.

Task 3 — performance. This function counts how often each target word appears. State its big-O, then rewrite it in O(n) and time both versions on 20,000 words.

def slow_count(words, targets):
    return {t: words.count(t) for t in targets}

Task 4 — safety. A teammate wrote this config loader. Name the two vulnerabilities, then rewrite it safely.

import pickle
settings = eval(open("settings.txt").read())
session = pickle.load(open("session.bin", "rb"))

Task 5 — choosing the tool (no code). For each workload, pick threads, multiprocessing, or asyncio, with a one-sentence reason. (a) Downloading 200 product images from a supplier API. (b) Generating 200 thumbnails from those images. (c) A notification server holding 10,000 idle websocket connections.

Solutions

Solution 1 (code/ch07/sol-01.py) — six tests covering the required cases plus one extra:

import re
import unittest


def slugify(title):
    """Turn 'Hello, World!' into 'hello-world' for use in URLs."""
    slug = title.lower()
    slug = re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9]+", "-", slug)
    return slug.strip("-")


class TestSlugify(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_basic_title(self):
        self.assertEqual(slugify("Hello World"), "hello-world")

    def test_punctuation_removed(self):
        self.assertEqual(slugify("Hello, World!"), "hello-world")

    def test_multiple_spaces_collapse(self):
        self.assertEqual(slugify("too   many    spaces"), "too-many-spaces")

    def test_leading_trailing_junk_stripped(self):
        self.assertEqual(slugify("  --Hi--  "), "hi")

    def test_empty_string(self):
        self.assertEqual(slugify(""), "")

    def test_already_a_slug(self):
        self.assertEqual(slugify("already-a-slug"), "already-a-slug")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main(verbosity=2)
test_already_a_slug (__main__.TestSlugify.test_already_a_slug) ... ok
test_basic_title (__main__.TestSlugify.test_basic_title) ... ok
test_empty_string (__main__.TestSlugify.test_empty_string) ... ok
test_leading_trailing_junk_stripped (__main__.TestSlugify.test_leading_trailing_junk_stripped) ... ok
test_multiple_spaces_collapse (__main__.TestSlugify.test_multiple_spaces_collapse) ... ok
test_punctuation_removed (__main__.TestSlugify.test_punctuation_removed) ... ok

----------------------------------------------------------------------
Ran 6 tests in 0.001s

OK

Solution 2 (code/ch07/sol-02.py) — the timeout is applied per task inside a wrapper, so one slow greeting cannot fail the others:

import asyncio


async def greet(name, delay):
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)  # simulated I/O
    return f"hello, {name}"


async def greet_all(names):
    async def greet_with_timeout(name, delay):
        try:
            return await asyncio.wait_for(greet(name, delay), timeout=0.5)
        except TimeoutError:
            return f"{name}: timed out, skipped"

    tasks = [asyncio.create_task(greet_with_timeout(n, d))
             for n, d in names]
    return await asyncio.gather(*tasks)


async def main():
    names = [("asha", 0.1), ("ravi", 0.4), ("meera", 2.0)]  # meera is too slow
    for line in await greet_all(names):
        print(line)


asyncio.run(main())
hello, asha
hello, ravi
meera: timed out, skipped

The key decision: wait_for wraps each greeting individually. Wrapping the whole gather in one wait_for would cancel everything when the slowest task timed out — including the greetings that were about to succeed.

Solution 3 (code/ch07/sol-03.py). slow_count is O(n²). list.count scans all n words, and it runs once per target (up to n targets). The fix counts everything in one pass:

import random
import time


def slow_count(words, targets):
    """O(n^2): one full scan per target."""
    return {t: words.count(t) for t in targets}


def fast_count(words, targets):
    """O(n): one pass builds the counts, then look each target up."""
    counts = {}
    for w in words:
        counts[w] = counts.get(w, 0) + 1
    return {t: counts.get(t, 0) for t in targets}


random.seed(7)
words = [random.choice(["apple", "banana", "cherry", "date"]) for _ in range(20_000)]
targets = words[:2_000]

start = time.perf_counter()
slow = slow_count(words, targets)
slow_t = time.perf_counter() - start

start = time.perf_counter()
fast = fast_count(words, targets)
fast_t = time.perf_counter() - start

assert slow == fast
print(f"slow (O(n^2)): {slow_t:.3f}s")
print(f"fast (O(n))  : {fast_t:.3f}s")
print(f"speedup: {slow_t / fast_t:.0f}x — same answer, less work")
slow (O(n^2)): 0.944s
fast (O(n))  : 0.005s
speedup: 191x — same answer, less work

Same pattern as the chapter example: a repeated linear scan hides inside the loop. One dict pass removes it.

Solution 4 (code/ch07/sol-04.py). There are two vulnerabilities. eval() on file contents executes anything in settings.txt. pickle.load() on session.bin executes code hidden in the bytes via __reduce__. The safe rewrite parses the settings as JSON, which is data only and never executed:

import json

# json.load only builds plain data: dicts, lists, strings, numbers.
# It can never execute code, so attacker input stays inert data.
settings_text = '{"theme": "dark", "retries": 3, "admin": false}'
settings = json.loads(settings_text)

theme = settings.get("theme", "light")
retries = settings.get("retries", 1)
if not isinstance(retries, int) or retries < 0:
    raise ValueError("retries must be a non-negative integer")

print("theme:  ", theme)
print("retries:", retries)
print("Loaded safely: json parsed data, it never runs it.")
theme:   dark
retries: 3
Loaded safely: json parsed data, it never runs it.

Note the extra step after parsing: validating the values (retries must be a non-negative int). Safe parsing stops code execution; validation stops bad data. You usually need both.

Solution 5:

  • (a) threads or asyncio. The work is waiting on the network, and the GIL is released during I/O waits, so 200 downloads overlap.
  • (b) multiprocessing. Thumbnail generation is pure CPU work. Threads would serialize on the GIL, while separate processes truly run in parallel.
  • (c) asyncio. 10,000 mostly-idle connections are thousands of concurrent waits on one thread. That's exactly what the event loop is built for, with none of the per-thread memory cost.

Chapter 8: Python for AI Applications

Most AI applications are ordinary Python with one unusual dependency: a model behind an HTTP API. The model part is a single call. Everything around it is the Python you already know. Retries and timeouts. Typed data. Generators for big datasets. asyncio for many calls at once. Tests that don't need the network. This chapter shows how those pieces fit when the thing on the other end of the wire is a large language model.

The examples use Claude through Anthropic's official anthropic SDK, plus NumPy for vector math and Pydantic for validation. Those three are the only third-party packages in the chapter. Everything else is the standard library.

Install them in a virtual environment, as in section 6.9:

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install anthropic numpy pydantic

The examples were verified with anthropic 1.15.0, numpy 2.5.4 and pydantic 2.14.1 on Python 3.13. The SDK's 1.x line is built on httpx2, which pip installs for you.

Every example runs offline. You don't need an API key to follow along. Where an example talks to Claude, it receives its client as an argument, and the __main__ block passes in a FakeAnthropic. That fake is the real anthropic.Anthropic class with the network unplugged: request building, response parsing, typed errors, retries and streaming all run through the real SDK code. Only the HTTP replies are canned. The helper lives in code/ch08/fakeclaude.py, and the end of section 8.2 walks through it. A comment in each example marks the one line that changes when you go live.

8.1 Talking to HTTP/JSON APIs: timeouts, retries, idempotency

Every model API is, underneath, an HTTP endpoint that takes JSON and returns JSON. So the first skill isn't AI at all. It's calling a remote service that is sometimes slow, sometimes busy and sometimes down, without your program hanging or falling over.

Four habits cover most of it.

Always set a timeout. Without one, a stalled connection can block your program forever. urllib.request.urlopen takes a timeout in seconds. The anthropic client defaults to 10 minutes, which suits long generations; you can lower it with anthropic.Anthropic(timeout=20.0).

Retry only what can succeed next time. A 429 (rate limited), a 5xx (server trouble) or a dropped connection is temporary. Wait and try again. A 400, 401, 403 or 404 means the request itself is wrong, and sending it again gives the same answer. Retrying those just burns time and quota.

Back off exponentially, with jitter. Double the wait after each failure, so a struggling server gets room to recover. Then randomize it. If a thousand clients fail at the same moment and all wait exactly one second, they all come back at the same moment too. "Full jitter" picks a random wait between zero and the exponential cap, which spreads them out. If the server sends a Retry-After header, respect it.

Make retries safe with idempotency. A retry is only harmless if repeating the request can't do the work twice. GET is naturally safe. A POST that charges a card is not: if the first attempt succeeded but the reply got lost, a blind retry charges again. The fix is an idempotency key. Generate one ID per logical operation, send it on every attempt, and let the server replay its earlier answer when it sees the key again.

The example below runs a small local server that fails twice with 503 before succeeding, and rejects malformed input with 400. The client retries the first case and gives up immediately on the second.

code/ch08/ex-01.py:

"""Chapter 8, example 1: calling a JSON API with timeouts, retries, and backoff.

A tiny local server stands in for a flaky remote API, so this runs offline.
"""
import http.server
import json
import random
import threading
import time
import urllib.error
import urllib.request
import uuid

RETRYABLE = {408, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504, 529}


class FlakyAPI(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    """Fails the first two calls with 503, then answers. Rejects bad input with 400."""
    calls = 0
    seen_keys = {}

    def do_POST(self):
        FlakyAPI.calls += 1
        body = json.loads(self.rfile.read(int(self.headers["Content-Length"])))
        key = self.headers.get("Idempotency-Key")
        if "text" not in body:
            return self.reply(400, {"error": "missing field: text"})
        if FlakyAPI.calls <= 2:
            return self.reply(503, {"error": "overloaded"}, {"Retry-After": "0"})
        if key in FlakyAPI.seen_keys:            # same key: replay, don't redo the work
            return self.reply(200, FlakyAPI.seen_keys[key])
        result = {"id": len(FlakyAPI.seen_keys) + 1, "words": len(body["text"].split())}
        FlakyAPI.seen_keys[key] = result
        self.reply(200, result)

    def reply(self, status, payload, headers=None):
        data = json.dumps(payload).encode()
        self.send_response(status)
        for name, value in (headers or {}).items():
            self.send_header(name, value)
        self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(data)))
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(data)

    def log_message(self, *args):                # keep the demo output quiet
        pass


def backoff_delay(attempt, base=0.05, cap=2.0, rng=random):
    """Exponential backoff with full jitter: a random wait in [0, base * 2**attempt]."""
    return rng.uniform(0, min(cap, base * 2 ** attempt))


def post_json(url, payload, *, timeout=5.0, max_attempts=4, rng=random):
    """POST JSON and return the decoded reply. Retries only failures worth retrying."""
    data = json.dumps(payload).encode()
    # One key for every attempt: the server can tell a retry from a new request.
    headers = {"Content-Type": "application/json", "Idempotency-Key": str(uuid.uuid4())}
    for attempt in range(max_attempts):
        request = urllib.request.Request(url, data=data, headers=headers, method="POST")
        try:
            with urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=timeout) as response:
                return json.load(response)
        except urllib.error.HTTPError as err:
            if err.code not in RETRYABLE:
                raise                            # 400, 401, 404...: retrying won't help
            retry_after = err.headers.get("Retry-After")
            reason = f"HTTP {err.code}"
        except (urllib.error.URLError, TimeoutError) as err:
            retry_after, reason = None, f"network: {err}"
        if attempt == max_attempts - 1:
            raise RuntimeError(f"gave up after {max_attempts} attempts ({reason})")
        delay = backoff_delay(attempt, rng=rng)
        if retry_after is not None:              # the server knows best
            delay = max(delay, float(retry_after))
        print(f"  attempt {attempt + 1} failed ({reason}); retrying in {delay:.3f}s")
        time.sleep(delay)


server = http.server.ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), FlakyAPI)
threading.Thread(target=server.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()
url = f"http://127.0.0.1:{server.server_port}/count"
rng = random.Random(8)                           # seeded so the output is repeatable

print("good request:")
print("  result:", post_json(url, {"text": "retry only what can succeed"}, rng=rng))

print("bad request:")
try:
    post_json(url, {"txt": "typo in the field name"}, rng=rng)
except urllib.error.HTTPError as err:
    print(f"  not retried: HTTP {err.code} {json.load(err)}")

print("delays for attempts 0-4:", [round(backoff_delay(a, rng=rng), 3) for a in range(5)])
print("server saw", FlakyAPI.calls, "calls")
server.shutdown()

Output:

good request:
  attempt 1 failed (HTTP 503); retrying in 0.011s
  attempt 2 failed (HTTP 503); retrying in 0.096s
  result: {'id': 1, 'words': 5}
bad request:
  not retried: HTTP 400 {'error': 'missing field: text'}
delays for attempts 0-4: [0.006, 0.07, 0.017, 0.099, 0.799]
server saw 4 calls

Read the output from the top. Two 503s, two short randomized waits, then success. The 400 fails on the first attempt: no retry, because nothing about the request would change. The last line of delays shows full jitter at work. The ceiling doubles each time (0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.8 seconds), but each actual wait is a random draw beneath it.

The seeded random.Random(8) exists only so the printed output repeats. In real code, use the module-level random functions.

Common mistakes. Retrying everything, including 400s, is the classic one. Close behind is retrying without a cap, so one bad dependency turns into an infinite loop. The quiet one is creating a new idempotency key on every attempt. That defeats the whole point: the server sees each retry as a brand-new request.

When you don't need this. Usually, when an SDK is involved. The anthropic client already retries connection errors, 408, 409, 429 and 5xx responses with exponential backoff, twice by default. You tune that with max_retries. Write your own retry loop for plain HTTP services, or when you need behaviour the SDK doesn't offer.

8.2 Calling Claude with the anthropic SDK

The SDK turns the Messages API into Python method calls and typed objects. One method does most of the work: client.messages.create().

Create the client with no arguments: anthropic.Anthropic(). It finds credentials itself, from the ANTHROPIC_API_KEY environment variable (or ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN, or a profile saved by ant auth login). Never paste a key into source code. Section 8.10 comes back to that.

A request needs three things:

  • model — which model to run. This chapter uses "claude-opus-5-5", the current default.
  • max_tokens — a hard ceiling on the length of the reply. It is a cap, not a target. If the model hits it, the reply is cut off mid-thought. Be generous: around 16,000 for an ordinary call, less only for deliberately tiny answers like a one-word label.
  • messages — the conversation so far, as a list of {"role": ..., "content": ...} dicts. It starts with a user turn. The API keeps no memory between calls, so you resend the whole history each time.

Two more parameters come up constantly. system sets standing instructions — who the model is, how to answer. And on Claude Opus 5.5, output_config={"effort": "low" | "medium" | "high" | "xhigh" | "max"} trades depth of reasoning against cost and speed. The default there is "medium".

The reply is a Message object, and its content is a list of typed blocks, not a string. A reply can hold a thinking block, one or more text blocks, and tool_use blocks when tools are involved (section 8.5). Opus 5.5 always thinks, but the thinking block's text stays empty unless you ask for a summary. So you check each block's type before you read it. response.content[0].text works in a demo and breaks the day a thinking block arrives first.

Two more fields matter on every call. stop_reason says why generation ended. "end_turn" is the normal finish. "max_tokens" means truncated. "tool_use" means the model wants a tool run. "refusal" means the model declined, and the content may be partial. And usage reports input_tokens and output_tokens, which is what you are billed for.

code/ch08/ex-02.py:

"""Chapter 8, example 2: one request to Claude, read properly.

Run offline with FakeAnthropic; swap in anthropic.Anthropic() for the real thing.
"""
import anthropic

from fakeclaude import FakeAnthropic, error_reply

MODEL = "claude-opus-5-5"


def ask(client: anthropic.Anthropic, question: str) -> str:
    response = client.messages.create(
        model=MODEL,
        max_tokens=16000,
        system="You are a concise Python tutor. Answer in two sentences.",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": question}],
    )
    print("stop_reason:", response.stop_reason)
    print("block types:", [block.type for block in response.content])
    print(f"usage: {response.usage.input_tokens} in, {response.usage.output_tokens} out")
    if response.stop_reason == "max_tokens":
        raise RuntimeError("answer was cut off; raise max_tokens or stream")
    # The reply is a list of typed blocks. Keep only the text ones.
    return "".join(block.text for block in response.content if block.type == "text")


def ask_safely(client: anthropic.Anthropic, question: str) -> str | None:
    """Most specific exception first; each class gets the handling it deserves."""
    try:
        return ask(client, question)
    except anthropic.BadRequestError as err:        # 400: our request is wrong
        print(f"fix the request: {err.status_code} {err.type}")
    except anthropic.AuthenticationError:           # 401: bad or missing key
        print("check ANTHROPIC_API_KEY")
    except anthropic.RateLimitError as err:         # 429: left after SDK retries
        print("rate limited; retry-after =", err.response.headers.get("retry-after"))
    except anthropic.APIStatusError as err:         # any other non-2xx
        print(f"API error {err.status_code}: {err.type}")
    except anthropic.APIConnectionError:            # never reached the server
        print("network problem")
    return None


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Production: client = anthropic.Anthropic()  # key from the environment
    reply = {
        "id": "msg_01", "type": "message", "role": "assistant", "model": MODEL,
        "content": [
            {"type": "thinking", "thinking": "", "signature": "sig-abc"},
            {"type": "text", "text": "A generator produces values lazily with yield. "
                                     "It keeps its state between calls to next()."},
        ],
        "stop_reason": "end_turn", "stop_sequence": None,
        "usage": {"input_tokens": 31, "output_tokens": 58},
    }
    client = FakeAnthropic([
        error_reply(529, "overloaded_error", "Overloaded"),     # retried by the SDK
        reply,
        error_reply(400, "invalid_request_error", "max_tokens: must be positive"),
    ])
    print(ask_safely(client, "What is a generator?"))
    print("HTTP requests sent:", len(client.sent))
    print()
    ask_safely(client, "And a coroutine?")

Output:

stop_reason: end_turn
block types: ['thinking', 'text']
usage: 31 in, 58 out
A generator produces values lazily with yield. It keeps its state between calls to next().
HTTP requests sent: 2

fix the request: 400 invalid_request_error

Look at "HTTP requests sent: 2". The script's first reply was a 529 (overloaded). The SDK retried it on its own, and ask never saw the failure. The second question hit a 400. The SDK raised BadRequestError at once, because a bad request stays bad.

The except chain runs from most specific to most general, as in section 6.5. Every class there is a subclass of anthropic.APIStatusError, except APIConnectionError, which covers failures before any response arrived. Catching only APIStatusError would work, but it throws away the one distinction that matters: retry later, or fix the code. Each error also carries .type, the API's own name for it ("rate_limit_error", "overloaded_error" and so on), and .status_code.

Common mistakes. Treating content as a string. Ignoring stop_reason and shipping a truncated answer as if it were complete. Setting max_tokens to a "typical" length instead of a ceiling. Creating a new client per request instead of reusing one; the client holds a connection pool.

Refusals in production. When Opus 5.5 declines a request, stop_reason is "refusal" and response.stop_details says why. You can let the API retry declined requests on a fallback model inside the same call. Use client.beta.messages.create(..., betas=["server-side-fallback-2026-07-01"], fallbacks="default"). Either way, check stop_reason before trusting the content.

How FakeAnthropic works

Here is the whole helper. It subclasses the real client and hands it an httpx2.MockTransport, a transport that calls a Python function instead of opening a socket. The function pops the next scripted reply. A dict becomes a 200 JSON response. An httpx2.Response passes through as is, which is how the error replies work. A callable gets to build its reply from the request. For streaming requests, the dict is re-encoded as the server-sent events the real API would send, one word per delta.

code/ch08/fakeclaude.py:

"""Chapter 8 helper: the real Anthropic SDK client with the network unplugged.

FakeAnthropic *is* anthropic.Anthropic. Only the HTTP transport is swapped for a
script of canned replies, so request building, response parsing, typed errors,
retries and streaming all run through the real SDK code.

    client = FakeAnthropic([text_reply("Hello!")])   # tests and this chapter
    client = anthropic.Anthropic()                   # production: key from env
"""
import asyncio
import json
import itertools

import anthropic
import httpx2

_ids = itertools.count(1)


def text_reply(text, *, input_tokens=12, output_tokens=None, stop_reason="end_turn"):
    """A Messages API response body holding one text block."""
    return _message([{"type": "text", "text": text}], stop_reason,
                    input_tokens, output_tokens or max(1, len(text.split())))


def tool_reply(name, tool_input, *, text=None, input_tokens=40, output_tokens=25):
    """A response body in which the model asks to call one tool."""
    blocks = [{"type": "text", "text": text}] if text else []
    blocks.append({"type": "tool_use", "id": f"toolu_{next(_ids):04d}",
                   "name": name, "input": tool_input})
    return _message(blocks, "tool_use", input_tokens, output_tokens)


def error_reply(status, error_type, message, headers=None):
    """An API error response: the SDK turns it into a typed exception."""
    body = {"type": "error", "error": {"type": error_type, "message": message}}
    return httpx2.Response(status, json=body, headers=headers or {})


def _message(content, stop_reason, input_tokens, output_tokens):
    return {"id": f"msg_{next(_ids):04d}", "type": "message", "role": "assistant",
            "model": "claude-opus-5-5", "content": content,
            "stop_reason": stop_reason, "stop_sequence": None,
            "usage": {"input_tokens": input_tokens, "output_tokens": output_tokens}}


def _sse(body):
    """Turn a full message body into the server-sent events a stream would carry."""
    def event(kind, data):
        return f"event: {kind}\ndata: {json.dumps({'type': kind, **data})}\n\n"
    start = {**body, "content": [], "stop_reason": None,
             "usage": {**body["usage"], "output_tokens": 1}}
    out = [event("message_start", {"message": start})]
    for i, block in enumerate(body["content"]):
        if block["type"] == "text":
            out.append(event("content_block_start", {"index": i, "content_block": {"type": "text", "text": ""}}))
            words = block["text"].split(" ")
            for n, word in enumerate(words):   # one delta per word, like tokens arriving
                piece = word if n == len(words) - 1 else word + " "
                out.append(event("content_block_delta", {"index": i, "delta": {"type": "text_delta", "text": piece}}))
        else:
            out.append(event("content_block_start", {"index": i, "content_block": {**block, "input": {}}}))
            out.append(event("content_block_delta", {"index": i, "delta": {
                "type": "input_json_delta", "partial_json": json.dumps(block["input"])}}))
        out.append(event("content_block_stop", {"index": i}))
    out.append(event("message_delta", {"delta": {"stop_reason": body["stop_reason"], "stop_sequence": None},
                                       "usage": {"output_tokens": body["usage"]["output_tokens"]}}))
    out.append(event("message_stop", {}))
    return httpx2.Response(200, content="".join(out).encode(),
                           headers={"content-type": "text/event-stream"})


class _Script:
    """Hands out canned replies in order and records every request body."""

    def __init__(self, replies):
        self.replies = list(replies)
        self.sent = []

    def respond(self, request):
        body = json.loads(request.content)
        if request.url.path.endswith("/count_tokens"):
            # Stand-in count (about 4 characters per token). The real endpoint
            # returns the model's exact count.
            return httpx2.Response(200, json={"input_tokens": len(json.dumps(body["messages"])) // 4})
        self.sent.append(body)
        if not self.replies:
            raise AssertionError("FakeAnthropic ran out of scripted replies")
        reply = self.replies.pop(0)
        if callable(reply):          # a function can build its reply from the request
            reply = reply(body)
        if isinstance(reply, httpx2.Response):
            return reply
        return _sse(reply) if body.get("stream") else httpx2.Response(200, json=reply)


class FakeAnthropic(anthropic.Anthropic):
    def __init__(self, replies, **options):
        self.script = _Script(replies)
        transport = httpx2.MockTransport(self.script.respond)
        super().__init__(api_key="sk-ant-fake", **options,
                         http_client=anthropic.DefaultHttpxClient(transport=transport))

    @property
    def sent(self):
        return self.script.sent


class AsyncFakeAnthropic(anthropic.AsyncAnthropic):
    """Async twin. `latency` seconds of simulated network time per request."""

    def __init__(self, replies, latency=0.0, **options):
        self.script = _Script(replies)
        self.in_flight = self.peak_in_flight = 0

        async def respond(request):
            self.in_flight += 1
            self.peak_in_flight = max(self.peak_in_flight, self.in_flight)
            try:
                await asyncio.sleep(latency)
                return self.script.respond(request)
            finally:
                self.in_flight -= 1

        super().__init__(api_key="sk-ant-fake", **options,
                         http_client=anthropic.DefaultAsyncHttpxClient(transport=httpx2.MockTransport(respond)))

    @property
    def sent(self):
        return self.script.sent

Two details are worth noticing. The fake records every request body in client.sent, which is what tests assert against. And it raises AssertionError when the script runs dry, so a test that makes one call too many fails loudly instead of hanging.

8.3 Streaming responses

A long answer can take many seconds to generate. Without streaming, your user stares at nothing until the last token is done. With streaming, the text arrives as it is produced, and the first words show up almost at once.

Streaming also protects you on the wire. A very long request with no data flowing can hit network idle timeouts. The SDK goes further: it refuses a non-streaming request whose max_tokens is so large it would likely run past ten minutes. For big outputs, stream.

client.messages.stream() is a context manager (section 6.3). Inside the with block, stream.text_stream is an iterator of text pieces, and stream.get_final_message() gives you the same Message object that create() would have returned. Leaving the block closes the connection, even if you stop early.

code/ch08/ex-03.py:

"""Chapter 8, example 3: streaming a reply as it is generated."""
import sys

import anthropic

from fakeclaude import FakeAnthropic, text_reply


def stream_answer(client: anthropic.Anthropic, prompt: str, out=sys.stdout) -> anthropic.types.Message:
    with client.messages.stream(
        model="claude-opus-5-5",
        max_tokens=64000,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
    ) as stream:
        for chunk in stream.text_stream:          # text deltas, in order
            out.write(chunk)
            out.flush()                           # show it now, not at exit
        message = stream.get_final_message()      # the same Message create() returns
    out.write("\n")
    return message
