            complete_task(tasks, 99)
        with self.assertRaises(TaskNotFoundError):
            remove_task(tasks, 99)

    def test_remove_drops_the_task(self):
        tasks = []
        add_task(tasks, "keep me")
        add_task(tasks, "drop me")
        removed = remove_task(tasks, 2)
        self.assertEqual(removed.title, "drop me")
        self.assertEqual([t.title for t in tasks], ["keep me"])

    # -- storage ----------------------------------------------------------

    def test_missing_store_file_means_no_tasks(self):
        self.assertEqual(load_tasks(self.store), [])

    def test_save_and_load_round_trip(self):
        tasks = []
        add_task(tasks, "round trip")
        complete_task(tasks, 1)
        save_tasks(self.store, tasks)

        loaded = load_tasks(self.store)
        self.assertEqual(loaded, tasks)  # dataclass __eq__ compares field by field
        self.assertTrue(loaded[0].done)

    def test_store_file_is_json(self):
        save_tasks(self.store, [Task(id=1, title="x", created="2026-01-01T00:00:00+00:00")])
        raw = json.loads(self.store.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
        self.assertEqual(raw[0]["title"], "x")

    def test_corrupt_json_raises_store_error(self):
        self.store.write_text("{ not json", encoding="utf-8")
        with self.assertRaises(StoreError):
            load_tasks(self.store)

    def test_non_list_json_raises_store_error(self):
        self.store.write_text('{"tasks": []}', encoding="utf-8")
        with self.assertRaises(StoreError):
            load_tasks(self.store)

    # -- CLI boundary -----------------------------------------------------

    def run_main(self, argv):
        """Run main(argv), capturing stdout/stderr; return (exit_code, out, err)."""
        out, err = io.StringIO(), io.StringIO()
        with redirect_stdout(out), redirect_stderr(err):
            code = main(argv)
        return code, out.getvalue(), err.getvalue()

    def test_main_add_then_list(self):
        code, out, _ = self.run_main(["add", "Buy milk"])
        self.assertEqual(code, 0)
        self.assertIn("added [1]: Buy milk", out)

        code, out, _ = self.run_main(["list"])
        self.assertEqual(code, 0)
        self.assertIn("[ ] 1: Buy milk", out)

    def test_main_list_empty(self):
        code, out, _ = self.run_main(["list"])
        self.assertEqual(code, 0)
        self.assertIn("No tasks yet", out)

    def test_main_done_and_remove(self):
        self.run_main(["add", "a"])
        self.run_main(["add", "b"])

        code, out, _ = self.run_main(["done", "1"])
        self.assertEqual(code, 0)
        self.assertIn("done [1]: a", out)

        code, out, _ = self.run_main(["remove", "2"])
        self.assertEqual(code, 0)
        self.assertIn("removed [2]: b", out)

        _, out, _ = self.run_main(["list"])
        self.assertIn("[x] 1: a", out)
        self.assertNotIn("b", out)

    def test_main_unknown_id_prints_error_and_exits_1(self):
        code, out, err = self.run_main(["done", "42"])
        self.assertEqual(code, 1)
        self.assertEqual(out, "")
        self.assertIn("error: no task with id 42", err)

    def test_tasks_survive_across_runs(self):
        self.run_main(["add", "persistent"])
        # A fresh load, as a new process would do:
        loaded = load_tasks(default_store_path())
        self.assertEqual([t.title for t in loaded], ["persistent"])


if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main()

A few test-design notes.

  • setUp gives every test a fresh temp directory and points TASKTRACKER_STORE at it. Tests never touch your real home directory and never interfere with each other.
  • The run_main helper is the payoff of main(argv) returning an int. The CLI gets tested like any other function, with stdout and stderr captured.
  • The exception tests use assertRaises as a context manager, the standard way to test that the right failure happens.
  • test_save_and_load_round_trip leans on the dataclass-generated __eq__. If to_dict/from_dict drop or mangle a field, the lists won't compare equal.

Sixteen tests, all green.

Design decisions, briefly

  • Dataclass for Task. A task is fixed-shape plain data. The decorator writes the boring methods (__init__, __repr__, __eq__) so the file shows only the interesting ones (to_dict, from_dict).
  • Exceptions raised in the middle, caught at the edge. Domain and storage functions raise specific errors; main() is the single place that turns them into user-facing output. Nothing is caught and swallowed — every raise either propagates to main or chains with from.
  • Storage as two functions, not a class. No state travels between calls, so a class would only add an __init__ storing the path. Functions keep the call graph flat and the tests obvious.
  • main(argv) returns an int. Testability. The process boundary (sys.exit) lives in the two-line __main__ block and nowhere else.
  • Env-var store path. Tests and examples get isolated storage without touching your real files. A tiny seam with an outsized payoff.

Where to go next

The program is finished but not done. A good codebase invites its next change. Each of these is a half-hour exercise that reuses a chapter of this guide:

  1. Priorities. Add an optional --priority flag to add (a Literal["low", "med", "high"] hint) and sort list by it. Touches Chapter 6 (type hints) and Chapter 2 (signatures).
  2. Atomic writes. Write to a temp file and os.replace it into place, so a crash mid-save can't leave half a JSON file. Touches the reliability half of the errors chapter.
  3. Search. Add a find <text> command using a generator expression over tasks. Touches Chapter 7 (iteration).
  4. Undo. Keep a backup of the previous store file on every save. Touches pathlib and thinking about failure modes.
  5. A --json flag for list. Machine-readable output for scripting. Touches the "program as a tool" mindset: stdout is an interface.

Part B — Back matter

Glossary

  • ABC — abstract base class. Declares an interface with abstract methods; can't be instantiated until a subclass implements them. Enforces "you must define this" at instantiation time.
  • annotation — a type hint on a variable, parameter, or return value. Stored in __annotations__, ignored by the runtime, read by checkers and tools.
  • argparse — the stdlib module for command-line interfaces. Declaratively turns argv into validated, typed arguments with --help for free.
  • argument — a value passed to a function at the call site. The parameter is the name in the definition; the argument is the value in the call.
  • assertion — a check that a condition holds, via assert. For invariants and tests, not for validating user input (asserts can be disabled with -O).
  • async/await — the coroutine syntax. await suspends the current coroutine and yields control to the event loop until the awaited work finishes.
  • attribute — a name bound to an object, reached with dot syntax: data attributes hold values, methods hold behavior.
  • callable — anything you can call with parentheses: functions, classes, bound methods, or instances defining __call__.
  • class — the blueprint for objects sharing behavior and initial state. Itself an object — an instance of its metaclass (usually type).
  • classmethod — a method bound to the class, not an instance. Receives cls; the standard way to write alternate constructors.
  • closure — a function that remembers its enclosing scope's variables even after that scope has finished executing.
  • comprehension — a one-expression loop building a list, set, or dict: [x*x for x in items if x > 0]. Prefer it over map/filter with lambdas for readability.
  • context manager — an object usable with with. Its __enter__/__exit__ (or a @contextmanager generator) guarantee cleanup, even when the body raises.
  • dataclass — a class decorator that generates __init__, __repr__, __eq__, and optionally ordering and hashing from annotated fields.
  • decorator — a callable that takes a function or class and returns a replacement, usually wrapping the original. @deco is shorthand for f = deco(f).
  • descriptor — an object defining __get__, __set__, or __delete__. Placed as a class attribute, it customizes what obj.attr does. property is one; functions are another.
  • duck typing — judging an object by the methods it supports rather than its class. "If it has read() and close(), it's file-like enough."
  • encoding — the scheme translating text to bytes and back (UTF-8 is the sane default). Must agree on write and read, or you get mojibake or UnicodeDecodeError.
  • exception — a runtime error represented as an object. Raised with raise, intercepted with try/except, and carrying a traceback of where it traveled.
  • f-string — a string literal with {expressions} evaluated inline at runtime. The default choice for formatting; faster to read than % or .format().
  • function — a named block of reusable code. In Python it's a first-class object: passable, returnable, storable, wrappable.
  • generator — a function containing yield. Calling it returns a lazy, single-use iterator that produces values on demand and remembers its position.
  • GIL — the Global Interpreter Lock. In standard CPython builds, only one thread runs Python bytecode at a time — which is why CPU-bound work wants processes, not threads. (3.13 ships an experimental free-threaded build; the GIL remains the default.)
  • hashable — safe to use as a dict key or set member. Requires __hash__ consistent with __eq__: objects that compare equal must hash equal.
  • immutable — value fixed at creation: int, str, tuple, frozenset. Immutable doesn't mean the variable can't be rebound — it means the object can't change.
  • inheritance — defining a class in terms of another, reusing and specializing its behavior. Powerful; also the easiest way to couple things that shouldn't be coupled.
  • iterator — an object with __next__ yielding items one at a time, raising StopIteration when done. Single-use by contract. (An iterable is anything iter() can turn into one.)
  • keyword argument — a call argument passed by name: f(key=value). Makes calls self-documenting; required after * in a signature.
  • lambda — a small anonymous function holding one expression. Handy as a sort key or callback; a def is clearer the moment it needs a name or a second line.
  • LEGB — the scope lookup order: Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in. The rule that decides which x a bare name refers to.
  • logging — the stdlib module for leveled diagnostic output (debug/info/warning/error). Configurable per module; what print wants to be when it grows up.
  • match statement — structural pattern matching (3.10+). Matches values against patterns — literals, shapes, types — with case arms and guards.
  • method — a function defined inside a class body. Accessed through an instance, a plain function becomes a bound method with self filled in automatically.
  • module — a single .py file and the unit of importing. Its top-level names become its attributes; __name__ is "__main__" when run as a script.
  • MRO — method resolution order. The C3-linearized chain of classes Python searches for an attribute; what super() follows.
  • mutable — value changeable in place: list, dict, set, bytearray. The source of aliasing surprises and the mutable-default-argument bug.
  • package — a directory of modules, importable as one dotted name. Modern Python doesn't require __init__.py (namespace packages), but having one is still conventional.
  • parameter — a name in a function definition that receives a value. Kinds: positional-only, positional-or-keyword, keyword-only, *args, **kwargs.
  • pathlib — the stdlib's object-oriented path library. Path replaces most os.path string juggling; / joins paths.
  • pickle — stdlib serialization of arbitrary objects to bytes. Convenient and dangerous: never unpickle untrusted data — it can execute arbitrary code during loading.
  • property — a data descriptor that turns method calls into attribute access. Computed attributes with validation, keeping the simple obj.x interface.
  • protocol — a typing construct for structural subtyping. Declares "has these members"; any class with them satisfies it, no inheritance required. Checked statically, invisible at runtime.
  • REPL — read-eval-print loop. The interactive >>> prompt; the fastest way to test a three-line hypothesis.
  • scope — the region of code where a name is visible and resolvable. Python has function, module, and built-in scopes, plus enclosing scopes for nested functions.
  • set — an unordered collection of unique hashable items. Membership tests are O(1); the right tool for "have I seen this" and deduplication.
  • signature — a function's full parameter contract: names, kinds, defaults, annotations. Introspectable via inspect.signature.
  • slots — __slots__ fixes an instance's attributes to a declared list, dropping the per-instance __dict__. Saves memory; trades away flexibility (no new attributes, subtle inheritance rules).
  • stdlib — the standard library: the modules shipped with every Python. argparse, json, pathlib, unittest, dataclasses all live here — no install needed.
  • subclass — a class inheriting from another. The parent is the superclass (or base class); substitutability means a subclass should be usable wherever the parent is expected.
  • super() — a proxy to the next class in the MRO. The cooperative way to extend a parent method rather than replacing it outright.
  • traceback — the printed stack of calls an exception traveled through, most recent call last. Read bottom-up: the last line names the error, the frames above show how you got there.
  • tuple — an immutable ordered sequence. The natural type for fixed-shape records like (x, y) coordinates or dict keys made of multiple values.
  • TypedDict — a typing construct declaring a dict's key names and value types. Purely static: at runtime it's still a plain dict with zero validation.
  • unittest — the stdlib testing framework. TestCase classes, assert* methods, and discovery that finds and runs every test_*.py file.
  • unpacking — binding an iterable's items to several names at once: x, y = point. Works in assignments, loops, and calls (f(*args)).
  • venv — a virtual environment: an isolated Python with its own installed packages. One per project keeps dependencies from fighting.
  • yield — the generator's pause button. Produces a value to the caller and freezes the function's state until the next __next__ resumes it.

Topic map: how the big ideas connect

The guide teaches its topics one chapter at a time, but they form a web, not a line. Here is the shape of it.

Everything starts with functions. In Python a function is an object like any other: you can pass it, return it, and store it.

A closure is what you get when a function refuses to forget. It's an inner function that keeps referencing its enclosing scope's variables after the outer function has returned. That remembered scope is the mechanism behind most decorators.

A decorator is a callable that takes a function and returns a new one. The standard way to build it is a closure. The outer call captures the decorator's arguments, the middle takes the function, and the inner wrapper runs before or after it. So functions, closures, and decorators are one lineage. Each chapter-2 idea grows directly out of the previous one.

Descriptors look unrelated until you see where they live: inside attribute access. Any object with __get__ (and optionally __set__/__delete__) can intercept obj.attr when placed as a class attribute. property is the descriptor you already know. It's a data descriptor that runs a method on access.

Plain functions are non-data descriptors. That's the quiet reason methods receive self without being asked. Accessing a function through an instance triggers its __get__, which binds the instance as the first argument. So descriptors are the machinery under classes, properties, and methods alike. The chapter-3 idea explains chapter-4 behavior you had been taking on faith.

Type hints are the thread running through the typing chapters. An annotation is inert at runtime; the interpreter stores it and moves on. But two different readers care about it.

Static checkers read hints to catch type errors before the program runs. And dataclasses read hints at class-creation time. The @dataclass decorator scans a class's annotations and generates __init__, __repr__, and __eq__ from them. A dataclass is literally a class decorator powered by type hints. The chapter-5 idea is chapters 3 and 6 combined.

TypedDict and Protocol are pure typing constructs. They exist for the checker and vanish at runtime. A TypedDict declares the shape of a dict (key names and value types) with no validation when the program runs. A Protocol declares a structural interface. Any class having the right members satisfies it, with no inheritance needed.

Both answer one question: how do I describe this precisely to a reader and a checker without changing runtime behavior? Classes are the things being described. Hints, TypedDicts, and Protocols are the descriptions.

The diagram below shows these relationships. Type hints sits at the center because nearly every other idea either uses them or is described by them.

Reading the map: follow the arrows. A function keeps its scope (closure); closures build decorators; decorators transform functions. Descriptors hook into class attribute lookup. The dataclass decorator adds methods to classes. Type hints define TypedDict shapes, describe Protocol structure, and declare dataclass fields; classes satisfy protocols structurally.

Review plan: spaced practice

Reading the guide once builds familiarity. Familiarity fades. What sticks is retrieval — pulling the ideas back out of your head on a schedule. Here is a concrete plan.

Day 2 — close the book and rebuild the small things. From memory, write three things:

  • a decorator with arguments (the three-level version)
  • a closure that demonstrates late binding, plus its fix
  • the Task dataclass with to_dict/from_dict

Then run them. Whatever you can't reproduce is what you didn't actually learn, so reread just those sections. Redo the Chapter 2 mutable-default exercise and the Chapter 7 generator-exhaustion exercise. Twenty minutes is enough; the point is retrieval, not rereading.

Week 1 — rebuild the capstone without looking. Delete your copy (keep the tests). Rewrite tasktracker.py from the spec: four commands, JSON persistence, the three exception types, errors caught only in main. Then run the original test file against your rewrite. Failing tests will point at exactly the design decisions you forgot, usually the exception boundary or default_factory.

Also explain MRO aloud in under two minutes. Then whiteboard the descriptor lookup path for obj.attr (instance dict → class → MRO → descriptor protocol). If you can't say it simply, you don't own it yet.

Week 4 — perform under mild pressure. Set a timer for 30 minutes. From scratch, write a context manager (both the class form and the @contextmanager form) and a generator pipeline with yield from. Then answer ten interview questions from the next section aloud, as if someone asked.

Finish by building one capstone extension from the "Where to go next" list. Pick the atomic-write one. It is the best test of whether the reliability ideas stuck. It forces you to think about what happens when the program dies halfway through a save.

Ongoing — the five-minute habits. Every time you write a function, ask: pure or effectful? Every time you catch an exception, ask: can I handle this, or am I hiding it? Every time you reach for a class, ask: does it carry state, or am I writing a namespace? Those three questions are the guide's judgment compressed into habit.

Interview questions

These test understanding, not recall. Each answer explains the reasoning an interviewer wants to hear.

1. After a = []; b = a; b.append(1), what is a? Why? a is [1]. Assignment never copies; it binds a name to an object. b = a makes both names point at the same list, so mutating through b is visible through a. If you needed independence, you'd copy explicitly (b = a.copy() or list(a)).

2. When should you use is instead of ==? == asks "equal value" (via __eq__); is asks "same object." Use is only for singletons like None. x is None is the idiom because there is exactly one None. Using is for value comparison (like x is 1000) sometimes works by accident, due to CPython caching small ints. That caching is an implementation detail, not a promise.

3. Why does def f(items=[]) accumulate items across calls? Default arguments are evaluated once, when the def executes, not per call. The same list object is reused as the default every time. The fix is the sentinel pattern: def f(items=None): items = [] if items is None else items. The root cause matches the dataclass default_factory lesson: definition-time evaluation.

4. This prints 4 4 4 4 4. Why, and how do you fix it?

funcs = [lambda: i for i in range(5)]
print([f() for f in funcs])

The lambdas close over the variable i, not its value at creation time. This is late binding. By the time they run, the loop has finished and i is 4. The fix is to bind the value as a default, lambda i=i: i, because defaults are evaluated at definition time.

5. What does @timer do to a function, mechanically? It's assignment: f = timer(f). timer receives the original function object and returns a new callable, usually a closure wrapping it. The name f is then rebound to the wrapper. That's why decorators can change behavior transparently. It's also why forgetting functools.wraps loses the original's name and docstring.

6. Why does a decorator with arguments need three levels of nesting? @retry(times=3) must first produce a decorator, and then that decorator wraps the function. So the outer function takes times and returns the decorator. The decorator takes func and returns the wrapper. The wrapper takes the call's arguments. Each level exists because each call happens at a different time: decoration time, then call time.

7. When is writing a raw descriptor better than using @property? When the same attribute logic must be reused across many classes or many attributes. A property is defined per class per attribute. A descriptor class (like a Validated or Typed descriptor) is written once and dropped into any class as a class attribute. If it's one attribute on one class, property is simpler. That's the whole decision.

8. Why do methods automatically receive self? Functions are non-data descriptors: they define __get__ but not __set__. When you access obj.method, the descriptor protocol calls function.__get__(obj, type(obj)). That returns a bound method with obj pre-filled as the first argument. self isn't magic syntax. It's the descriptor protocol doing its job.

9. In a diamond inheritance (D(B, C), both inherit A), which parent's method wins, and why is the answer predictable? Python linearizes the hierarchy with C3 into one MRO: D, B, C, A, object. Attribute lookup walks that single chain in order, so B's method wins over C's and A's. The answer is predictable because of two C3 guarantees. Every class appears after its subclasses, and local declaration order is preserved. super() follows this same chain.

10. You define __eq__ on a class and suddenly instances can't be dict keys. What happened? Defining __eq__ without __hash__ makes Python set __hash__ to None. The class becomes unhashable. The rule is that equal objects must hash equal, and a mutable object with value-based equality can't promise a stable hash. If you need hashing, use @dataclass(frozen=True), which generates both consistently. Or define __hash__ deliberately.

11. What does frozen=True on a dataclass actually guarantee? It blocks attribute reassignment (obj.x = 1 raises FrozenInstanceError). It does not freeze the contents of mutable fields. A frozen dataclass holding a list can still have that list mutated. Frozen means "can't rebind fields," not "deeply immutable."

12. You annotate a function to take a TypedDict and pass a dict with a wrong value type. What happens at runtime? Nothing. TypedDict is purely static. At runtime the annotation is ignored and the value is a plain dict. There's no validation and no error. If you need runtime validation, you build it yourself (or use a library). TypedDict was never that tool.

13. What's the practical difference between annotating a parameter Any and object? Any tells the checker to stop checking: any operation is allowed, with no errors ever. object tells the truth: "I know nothing about this." So the checker forces you to narrow it (usually with isinstance) before doing anything specific. Any is convenient and contagious; object is honest.

14. Why does the type checker accept x + 1 after if isinstance(x, int) when x was str | int? Narrowing. isinstance is one of the constructs checkers understand. Inside the if branch, the declared union is narrowed to int, so the operation type-checks. In the else branch it's narrowed to str. The annotation didn't change. The checker's knowledge did, based on a runtime test it can reason about.

15. Why does the second list(gen) return []? A generator is a single-use iterator. The first list() drives it to exhaustion, and there's no rewind. The generator function can be called again to make a fresh generator. But the generator object is spent. If you need the data twice, materialize it into a list once.

16. What does yield from give you that a manual for loop doesn't? Delegation. yield from subgen() yields every value from the sub-generator. It also passes the sub-generator's return value back as the expression's value. A manual loop drops the return value on the floor. yield from also forwards send()/throw() into the sub-generator, which a loop can't do.

17. If the body of a with block raises, does cleanup still run? What if __exit__ returns a true value? Yes. That's the entire point of context managers: __exit__ runs on the exception path too. If __exit__ returns a truthy value, it suppresses the exception, and the with statement exits normally. A falsy return re-raises it. Suppress deliberately and rarely. Swallowing exceptions silently is a debugging nightmare.

18. What's wrong with wrapping a large block in except Exception: pass? It hides every failure, including bugs you haven't thought of: NameError from a typo, KeyboardInterrupt (well, that's BaseException), real logic errors. You lose the traceback. The program continues in a state you can't reason about, and the bug surfaces far from its cause. Catch what you can actually handle, as narrowly as possible, and let the rest propagate.

19. Why write raise StoreError(...) from exc instead of a bare raise StoreError(...)? Chaining preserves the causal chain. With from exc, the traceback shows both the original error (the JSONDecodeError) and the higher-level one, with "directly caused by" between them. A bare re-raise leaves you guessing what the low-level failure was. Chaining keeps the evidence.

20. Module a imports b, and b imports a, and you get an ImportError on a partially initialized module. What's happening, and what's the standard fix? Python executes a module's top-level code on first import. a starts importing b, and b starts importing a. At that point a is only half-executed, so the names b wants don't exist yet. There are two fixes. Move one import inside the function that needs it, deferring it until call time. Or restructure so the shared names live in a third module both import.

21. CPU-bound number crunching: threads, processes, or asyncio? Why? Processes. In standard CPython the GIL lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time. So threads can't parallelize CPU work. (They help with I/O-bound work, where threads wait while others run.) asyncio is single-threaded cooperation: great for many waiting connections, useless for computation. Processes each get their own interpreter and GIL, so they genuinely run in parallel. The price is heavier startup and explicit data passing.

22. What does await actually do to the event loop? It suspends the current coroutine and returns control to the loop. The loop runs other ready coroutines until the awaited thing completes. Nothing blocks: one thread, many tasks taking turns. That's why await inside a coroutine is cheap. Calling a blocking function (like time.sleep) inside one freezes everything, because it never yields.

23. Why is pickle.loads on untrusted data a security hole? Unpickling isn't just reading data. It can construct arbitrary objects and call callables during loading. A crafted pickle payload executes attacker code on loads. Never unpickle data you didn't produce. For untrusted input, use json or another format that only builds plain data.

24. Same question for eval on user input. eval executes its argument as Python code with your program's privileges. "User input" becomes "user's program running inside yours," with file access, imports, everything. If you need to parse user-supplied data, use json.loads or ast.literal_eval. The latter only builds literals and never executes.

Coverage checklist

Every topic promised in the guide's scope is verified present here. Sections map to chapters in order. Chapter 5 carries both dataclasses and type hints. Chapter 6 carries iteration together with errors, modules, and everyday tooling. Chapter 7 is the testing and concurrency chapter. Chapter 8 applies them to AI applications, and Chapter 9 is the capstone.

1. Python foundations — ✓ Chapter 1

  • running Python / REPL / scripts / modules / project setup
  • names / objects / references / assignment / identity / equality / copying
  • core types: numbers / strings / bytes / booleans / None / lists / tuples / dicts / sets
  • mutability / truthiness / comparisons / operators / conversion pitfalls
  • expressions / statements / conditions / loops / match / comprehensions

2. Functions — ✓ Chapter 2

  • definition / call / returns / early returns
  • positional-only / positional-or-keyword / keyword-only params
  • defaults incl. mutable-default bug
  • *args / **kwargs
  • unpacking / binding / signatures
  • LEGB / global / nonlocal
  • nested functions / closures / late binding
  • lambda / higher-order / first-class
  • recursion

3. Decorators/descriptors — ✓ Chapter 3

  • decorator as callable transform from function-call model
  • simple decorator then decorator with own arguments
  • closures / wrapper signatures / functools.wraps / order / debugging
  • descriptor protocol __get__ / __set__ / __delete__ via attribute lookup
  • data vs non-data descriptors, properties / methods fit
  • small descriptor example + when property is simpler
  • connection to class/instance attrs, methods, classmethod, staticmethod
  • value and cost, not everyday requirement

4. OOP — ✓ Chapter 4

  • classes / instances / attrs / self / init / lifecycle
  • instance / class / staticmethods / properties / encapsulation conventions
  • inheritance / overriding / substitutability / composition vs inheritance
  • MI / MRO / super() / cooperative init
  • ABCs vs Protocol, when each helps
  • special methods __repr__ / __str__ / __eq__ / __hash__ / __iter__ / context-manager methods
  • equality + hashing rules for dict keys / set members
  • __slots__ changes / trade-offs / when to avoid
  • design mistakes (deep inheritance, hidden base-class state, unnecessary abstractions)

5. Dataclasses/TypedDict — ✓ Chapter 5

  • dataclass generated methods / defaults / default_factory / __post_init__ / frozen / ordering / slots / equality
  • mutable-field pitfalls + frozen guarantees
  • TypedDict required / optional / total / Required / NotRequired / inheritance

6. Type hints — ✓ Chapter 5
